digital-citizens-rights.certificationPath: L1 Basic identity verification → L2 GDPR compliant identity processing → L3 eIDAS 2.0 aligned digital identity → L4 Full EU Digital Identity Wallet compliance → L5 Autonomous citizen rights governance with verified sovereignty and contestability

complianceFrameworkRefs.label: EU AI Act Art. 5; Annex III point 1(a)/5(a)

complianceFrameworks: EU AI Act Art. 5; Annex III point 1(a)/5(a)
digital-citizens-rights.description: Citizen data tied with digital identity and tagged with government identities — supporting tax, travel documents, and rights to private and secure data — AI agents managing digital identity ecosystems, citizen data rights, and public trust infrastructure.
digital-citizens-rights.euAIActClassification: Annex III §1(a) — remote biometric identification (biometric verification that only confirms a claimed identity is excluded) and §5(a) — where identity gates public assistance benefits; Annex III obligations apply from 2 Dec 2027; PROHIBITED under Art. 5(1)(c), (g), (h) where those practices apply now
keyRisks: Mass surveillance through digital identity AI integration
Identity fraud amplification through AI-weakened verification
Exclusion of vulnerable populations from digital identity systems
Government data abuse enabled by AI identity correlation
Loss of anonymous participation rights through identity AI requirements
digital-citizens-rights.name: Digital Citizens & Rights

questions.failureMode: The agent accepts a substantial-level login as sufficient for a transaction that requires assurance level high and issues an identity attribute to an impostor.
questions.l1: No eIDAS compliance; digital identity verification does not meet eIDAS assurance levels (low/substantial/high) or EU Digital Identity Wallet requirements
questions.l2: Assurance levels are named in design documents, but the agent does not check which level a verification actually reached before it acts
questions.l3: Agent implements eIDAS assurance level verification for core use cases, but does not support EU Digital Identity Wallet integration or Art. 6a wallet-based identity attestation
questions.l4: Assurance-level checks and wallet-based attestation run in production with selective disclosure, but cross-border recognition or qualified electronic signature flows are not evidenced per release
questions.l5: Full eIDAS 2.0 compliance with EU Digital Identity Wallet integration, Art. 8 assurance level high verification, qualified electronic signature support, selective disclosure of identity attributes, and cross-border recognition per Art. 6a
questions.remediation: Add a pre-action check that reads the assurance level (low, substantial, high) of the presented identity and blocks any identity transaction whose required level is not met, logging the level achieved.
questions.text: Does the agent implement EU eIDAS 2.0 Regulation 2024/1183 Article 6a European Digital Identity Wallet requirements for identity verification assurance levels?

questions.failureMode: The agent, asked to find a person in station camera feeds, runs real-time remote identification on public-space video with no prior-authorisation reference on record.
questions.l1: Neither practice is screened: the agent can be configured or invoked to infer sensitive traits from biometric data or to run real-time remote identification in public spaces, and no use-case record shows an Art. 5 assessment
questions.l2: Both practices are named in written policy, but use-case intake never asks whether a request involves biometric categorisation or real-time remote identification
questions.l3: Both practices are prohibited in written policy and screened at use-case intake, but at most one of them is blocked technically at runtime, or exceptions are granted without a recorded prior-authorisation reference
questions.l4: Both practices are blocked at runtime and releases need a prior-authorisation reference, but no named owner reviews the block-and-release log each release
questions.l5: Both practices are blocked at runtime; a real-time identification request is released only with a recorded Art. 5(3) prior-authorisation reference for an Art. 5(1)(h) objective; every block and release is logged, and the log is reviewed by a named owner each release
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(g), 5(1)(h), 5(2)-(3) (apply from 2 Feb 2025); Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices (4 Feb 2025, non-binding)
questions.remediation: Put a tool-level allowlist in front of the biometric functions that rejects categorisation and real-time remote identification calls unless the request carries a recorded Art. 5(3) prior-authorisation reference, and log every block and release.
questions.text: Does the agent block the two EU AI Act prohibited biometric practices that identity systems can be repurposed for: biometric categorisation that infers race, political opinions, trade-union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation (Art. 5(1)(g)), and use of 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement outside the objectives and prior authorisation set by Art. 5(1)(h) and 5(2)-(3)?

questions.failureMode: The agent is redeployed with a new name-matching model that rejects more non-Latin-script names, and no assessment catches the impact on minority-language citizens before go-live.
questions.l1: No human rights impact assessment exists for any AI use case that affects citizens
questions.l2: A human rights risk note exists for some AI use cases, but it does not identify affected groups or list mitigations
questions.l3: An assessment was done once before deployment with identified risks and mitigations, but it is not repeated on change, mitigations are not tracked to closure, or affected groups were not consulted
questions.l4: Assessments are repeated on each material change with affected-group input and mitigations tracked to closure, but grievance cases are not yet cited in the next assessment
questions.l5: Assessment per use case, repeated on each material change and at a set interval, with input from affected groups, mitigations tracked to closure, and grievance cases from an operating channel cited in the next assessment
questions.regulatoryRef: UNGPs Principles 17-21, 29; CoE AI Convention Art. 16
questions.remediation: Gate each agent release that changes identity-service behaviour on a refreshed human rights impact assessment, with open mitigations blocking the release until closed or accepted by a named owner.
questions.text: Before an AI system that affects citizens' rights goes live, and again on each material change, does the operator carry out a human rights impact assessment that identifies affected groups, assesses the impacts, tracks each mitigation to closure and feeds grievance cases back into the next assessment (UN Guiding Principles 17-21; CoE AI Convention Art. 16 risk and impact management framework)?

questions.failureMode: The agent keeps answering from a cached copy of a citizen's old identity record after the register was rectified, because the correction never reached its retrieval index.
questions.l1: Identity-data access, rectification or erasure requests are not routed or answered
questions.l2: Some access, rectification or erasure requests reach the right team, but there is no single intake and many are answered ad hoc
questions.l3: Requests are routed and answered, but response times are not measured against the Art. 12(3) period, or refusals are not recorded with a legal basis
questions.l4: Every request is logged with dates and any refusal basis inside the Art. 12(3) period, but rectifications are not shown to reach every system the agent reads from
questions.l5: Every request is logged with receipt date, identity check, action taken, response date within the Art. 12(3) period and any refusal basis; rectifications propagate to every system the agent reads from, with evidence per request
questions.remediation: Route every identity-data request into a register that starts the Art. 12(3) clock at receipt, and add a propagation check that confirms a rectification has reached each source the agent reads before the case closes.
questions.text: Does the agent route and fulfil citizens' requests to access, rectify and erase government-held digital identity data (GDPR Arts 15-17) within the one-month period of GDPR Art. 12(3), recording any refusal based on a lawful retention duty with its legal basis?

questions.failureMode: The agent answers an identity-service phone line in a human-sounding voice and never says it is an AI system, so callers share details believing they are speaking to an official.
questions.l1: No AI-interaction disclosure on any channel
questions.l2: Disclosure is given on the main web chat only; voice, email and form channels carry none
questions.l3: Disclosure exists only in terms of service or a footer, or only on some channels
questions.l4: Plain-language disclosure is given at first interaction on every channel and logged per session, but accessible formats or per-release re-tests are missing
questions.l5: Plain-language disclosure at first interaction on every channel, in accessible formats, logged per session, and re-tested on each release
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 50(1), 50(5); CoE AI Convention Art. 15(2)
questions.remediation: Make the first turn on every identity-service channel a fixed disclosure injected by the channel adapter rather than the model, and fail the release test if any channel session starts without the logged disclosure.
questions.text: On every identity-service channel (chat, voice, email, forms), is the agent designed so that people are told they are interacting with an AI system, clearly and distinguishably, at the latest at the first interaction (EU AI Act Art. 50(1) and 50(5), applicable from 2 Aug 2026; CoE AI Convention Art. 15(2))?

questions.failureMode: The agent repeatedly asks a blind applicant to complete a visual liveness check and closes the enrolment as failed instead of offering an assisted channel.
questions.l1: No digital inclusion; digital identity systems are inaccessible to persons with disabilities, elderly citizens, and those without digital skills
questions.l2: Some identity screens were checked against WCAG 2.1 AA, but the agent-driven journey has known blocking failures and no non-digital route
questions.l3: Agent implements WCAG 2.1 AA for digital identity interfaces, but does not provide alternative access channels or implement full CRPD Art. 9 accessibility requirements
questions.l4: Digital journeys meet WCAG 2.1 AA and a staffed non-digital route exists, but assisted enrolment or digital-literacy support for vulnerable populations is not in place
questions.l5: Full digital inclusion with WCAG 2.1 AA+ implementation, CRPD Art. 9 multi-channel access (digital and non-digital), assisted identity enrollment for vulnerable populations, digital literacy support, and universal design per EU Accessibility Directive
questions.regulatoryRef: CRPD Art. 9; EU Web Accessibility Directive 2016/2102
questions.remediation: Add an escalation tool the agent must call after two failed identity-verification attempts or on an accessibility cue, handing the citizen to assisted or in-person enrolment instead of ending the session.
questions.text: Does the agent implement digital inclusion safeguards per UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) Article 9 accessibility and EU Web Accessibility Directive for digital identity services?

questions.failureMode: The agent changes the bank account registered for a citizen's tax refund on the strength of an SMS one-time code, a session level below what the mapping requires for that transaction.
questions.l1: High-risk identity transactions accept single-factor or SMS-only authentication and no assurance-level mapping exists
questions.l2: Multi-factor authentication exists for some transactions, but high-risk transactions can still complete with SMS-only codes and no mapping is written down
questions.l3: Multi-factor authentication is used, but the mapping from transaction type to assurance level is missing or incomplete, or the authenticators used do not meet the mapped level
questions.l4: Every transaction type is mapped to a level per scheme and authenticators meet it, but the level achieved is not recorded per event or the mapping is not re-reviewed on scheme changes
questions.l5: A documented mapping assigns every transaction type an assurance level under each applicable scheme; authenticators meet the mapped level's requirements; each authentication event records the level achieved; the mapping is reviewed when NIST, ISO or eIDAS implementing acts change
questions.regulatoryRef: eIDAS 2.0 Art. 8 (assurance levels); NIST SP 800-63B-4 (July 2025, supersedes SP 800-63B); ISO/IEC 29115:2013
questions.remediation: Store the transaction-to-assurance-level mapping as configuration the agent reads before each identity action, and step the citizen up to a stronger authenticator when the session's achieved level is below the mapped one.
questions.text: Does the agent authenticate citizens for identity services at an assurance level matched to each transaction's risk, using a documented mapping to eIDAS assurance levels (low, substantial, high) in EU flows, NIST SP 800-63B-4 authenticator assurance levels in US federal flows, and ISO/IEC 29115:2013 levels of assurance, and does it apply the authenticator requirements of the mapped level, including the highest level where the mapping requires it?

questions.failureMode: The agent keeps issuing attestations from a compromised credential store and treats the spike in failed verifications as user error, so no breach timer starts.
questions.l1: No identity breach response; identity system incidents are handled without GDPR Art. 33 notification timelines or NIS2 significant incident escalation procedures
questions.l2: Identity incidents are handled ad hoc by the security team; the agent neither detects anomalies nor starts any notification clock
questions.l3: Agent detects identity system anomalies and can initiate breach notification, but does not automate GDPR Art. 33 72-hour notification or NIS2 Art. 23 competent authority reporting
questions.l4: Art. 33 and NIS2 Art. 23 notifications are drafted automatically within their timelines, but credential revocation or holder notification under Art. 34 still depends on manual steps
questions.l5: Full identity incident response with automated GDPR Art. 33 notification within 72 hours, NIS2 Art. 23 significant incident reporting, affected identity holder notification per Art. 34, credential revocation workflows, and forensic-ready audit evidence preservation
questions.remediation: Have the agent open an incident record with a 72-hour Art. 33 timer as soon as an identity-compromise signal fires, suspend the affected credentials pending human confirmation, and preserve the related logs.
questions.text: Does the agent implement breach notification and identity compromise response per GDPR Article 33 72-hour notification and EU NIS2 Directive Article 23 for identity infrastructure incidents?

questions.failureMode: The agent ranks applicants for faster public-service processing using their parking-fine and library-overdue history pulled from linked identity records.
questions.l1: No social-scoring screen: the agent can build or apply behaviour-based scores to identity holders
questions.l2: Social scoring is mentioned in an acceptable-use policy, but use cases are not screened and the agent can compute behaviour scores on request
questions.l3: Social scoring is prohibited in policy and use cases are screened at intake, but no runtime check stops a scoring request or a score from being used across contexts
questions.l4: Runtime rules block cross-context use of behaviour scores and blocks are logged, but intake records no guideline-based Art. 5(1)(c) assessment or blocks are not reviewed each release
questions.l5: Use-case intake records a guideline-based Art. 5(1)(c) assessment; runtime rules block cross-context use of behaviour scores; blocked requests are logged and reviewed each release
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(c) (applies from 2 Feb 2025); Commission Guidelines on prohibited AI practices (4 Feb 2025, non-binding)
questions.remediation: Tag every identity-holder attribute with its source context and add a runtime rule that refuses any ranking or eligibility tool call combining behaviour-derived attributes across contexts, logging the refusal.
questions.text: Does the agent refuse to evaluate or classify people over time based on their social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal characteristics where the resulting score leads to detrimental treatment in unrelated contexts or treatment disproportionate to the behaviour (EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(c) social scoring), including when it is asked to rank identity holders for access to public services?

questions.failureMode: The agent processes a wallet recovery request after a chat-based knowledge check and re-binds a high-assurance wallet to a device the fraudster controls.
questions.l1: No Art. 5a wallet control: wallet assurance level high is not defined, evidenced, or auditably enforced
questions.l2: Wallet features such as selective disclosure are planned or piloted, but assurance level high is not defined for any wallet flow
questions.l3: Some wallet features exist (e.g., selective disclosure), but assurance level high governance and evidence are incomplete or non-auditable
questions.l4: Assurance level high is governed and evidenced for issuance and authentication, but relying-party verification, cross-border acceptance or suspension, revocation and recovery lack auditable evidence
questions.l5: Full Art. 5a EUDI Wallet implementation with assurance level high governance, relying-party verification, cross-border acceptance, and auditor-ready evidence packs for issuance/authentication/attestation lifecycles
questions.regulatoryRef: eIDAS 2.0 Art. 5a (EUDI Wallet), assurance level high
questions.remediation: Before the agent completes a wallet issuance, recovery or revocation step, require the high-assurance evidence bundle (issuance, authentication, attribute attestation) and write the lifecycle event with its bundle id.
questions.text: Does the agent implement eIDAS 2.0 Article 5a EU Digital Identity Wallet requirements with explicit support for wallet assurance level high, including (1) assurance claim governance, (2) evidence bundles for high assurance (issuance + authentication + attribute attestation), (3) relying-party verification flows, (4) cross-border acceptance checks, and (5) auditable wallet lifecycle controls (issuance, suspension, revocation, recovery)?

questions.failureMode: The agent's matching function is extended from one-to-one verification to one-to-many search without re-classification, so it runs as remote biometric identification with no risk or oversight record.
questions.l1: Use cases are not classified against Annex III, or a high-risk use case has none of the Art. 9-14 artefacts
questions.l2: Some use cases are labelled high-risk, but there is no written classification rationale and none of the Art. 9-14 artefacts exist
questions.l3: Each use case is classified with a rationale, and some artefacts exist (e.g. logs, documentation), but risk-management or data-governance evidence is missing
questions.l4: Classification and the full Art. 9-14 artefact set exist, but artefacts are not versioned with each agent release or open gaps are not dated against 2 Dec 2027
questions.l5: Classification per use case with rationale (including any reliance on the Annex III 1(a) verification exclusion); the complete Art. 9-14 artefact set is versioned with each agent release; open gaps are tracked against 2 Dec 2027
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Annex III point 1(a), point 5(a); EU AI Act Art. 9-12, 14; EU AI Act Art. 113 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Annex III high-risk obligations from 2 Dec 2027)
questions.remediation: Add a release gate that refuses to ship an agent version for an Annex III use case unless its classification record and versioned Art. 9-14 artefact index match the release tag.
questions.text: Where the agent is, or is part of, a high-risk AI system under EU AI Act Annex III in this pack's scope — remote biometric identification (point 1(a); biometric verification that only confirms a claimed identity is excluded) or eligibility for essential public assistance benefits (point 5(a)) — does it hold the Chapter III Section 2 evidence set (risk management Art. 9, data governance Art. 10, technical documentation Art. 11, record-keeping Art. 12, human oversight Art. 14), with a gap plan dated against 2 Dec 2027, when those obligations apply to Annex III systems?

questions.failureMode: The agent shares a citizen's health-condition attribute with a housing office on the strength of a blanket onboarding consent the citizen had already withdrawn.
questions.l1: No explicit-consent controls: special-category attributes are processed/shared without explicit consent evidence or withdrawal handling
questions.l2: Consent is a single checkbox at wallet onboarding that covers every attribute and purpose
questions.l3: Consent is captured, but is not granular/purpose-scoped or lacks auditable receipts and withdrawal enforcement
questions.l4: Granular, purpose-scoped consent with receipts and withdrawal enforcement is in place, but safeguards against coerced consent in public-service contexts are not tested
questions.l5: Full Art. 9(2)(a) explicit-consent governance with granular consent receipts, withdrawal enforcement, and audit-ready logs tied to attribute disclosure events
questions.remediation: Require a live, purpose-matched consent receipt for the specific special-category attribute before the agent's disclosure tool releases it, and make withdrawal revoke the receipt so the next call fails.
questions.text: When special-category attributes are stored or shared via the digital identity wallet, does the agent implement GDPR Art. 9(2)(a) explicit consent with (1) purpose-scoped consent prompts, (2) granular attribute-level consent, (3) withdrawal/refresh rules, (4) consent receipt + audit logs, and (5) safeguards against coerced consent in public-service contexts?

questions.failureMode: The agent lets a citizen bind a new authenticator through an emailed link, a recovery path weaker than the AL3 proofing the account was created under.
questions.l1: No AL3 mapping: assurance controls are inconsistent and cannot be evidenced against §7 AL3
questions.l2: Strong authentication is used on some services, but no service is mapped to AL3 and identity proofing strength varies between them
questions.l3: Some strong auth controls exist, but AL3 mapping and audit evidence are incomplete
questions.l4: Wallet and service flows are mapped to AL3 and enforced consistently, but binding and recovery paths or auditor evidence packs are incomplete
questions.l5: Full §7 AL3 operationalization with clear control mapping, consistent enforcement, and auditor-ready evidence packs
questions.remediation: Map each service's proofing, authenticator and recovery steps to the AL3 requirements, and add a test that fails if any agent-reachable recovery path binds a new authenticator below AL3.
questions.text: Does the agent implement ISO/IEC 29115:2013 §7 assurance level AL3 for entity authentication (and map wallet flows to AL3), including identity proofing strength, authenticator requirements, binding/recovery, phishing resistance expectations appropriate to AL3, and evidence for auditors that AL3 controls are consistently applied across services?

questions.failureMode: The agent tells a relying party that a wallet requirement comes from a superseded eIDAS article, so the operator builds controls against the wrong text.
questions.l1: No mapping governance: citations drift and requested anchors (e.g., Art. 5a) are not consistently used
questions.l2: A spreadsheet maps some controls to eIDAS articles, but it is not versioned and Art. 5a anchors are missing where required
questions.l3: Mapping exists but updates are manual and inconsistently applied
questions.l4: The mapping is versioned and reviewed on regulatory updates, but citation consistency across questions and agent outputs is checked by hand
questions.l5: Versioned, reviewed control mapping with automated citation-consistency checks and audit-defensible references
questions.remediation: Add an automated check that compares every eIDAS citation in agent prompts, outputs and evidence exports with the versioned control-to-article map and fails the build on a mismatch.
questions.text: Does the program maintain a versioned eIDAS 2.0 control-to-article mapping for the EUDI Wallet (ensuring Art. 5a anchors are used where required), with review on regulatory updates and automated checks for citation consistency across questions and outputs?

questions.failureMode: The agent answers an explanation request with a generic description of the model instead of the inputs and output that drove the refusal of this person's identity application.
questions.l1: Affected persons cannot obtain any explanation of the AI system's role
questions.l2: A request route exists, but staff can only confirm that an AI system was involved, with no detail of its role
questions.l3: Explanations are given on request, but they are generic and not specific to the decision
questions.l4: Decision-specific explanations are built from logged inputs and outputs, but delivery is not time-bound or not linked to any later appeal
questions.l5: Decision-specific explanations generated from logged inputs and outputs, delivered in plain language within a set time, and tracked through to any appeal
questions.remediation: Log each high-risk decision's inputs, model output and human action under a decision id, and generate the plain-language explanation from that record when the affected person asks.
questions.text: When a decision based on the output of an Annex III high-risk AI system produces legal effects for a person, can the affected person obtain a clear and meaningful explanation of the AI system's role and the main elements of the decision, as EU AI Act Article 86 provides?

questions.failureMode: The agent suspends a citizen's digital identity after a fraud flag and handles the citizen's objection itself, re-confirming its own decision with no human review.
questions.l1: No route to contest AI-influenced identity decisions
questions.l2: Citizens can complain through a general channel, but it is not linked to the AI-influenced decision or reviewed by a human able to change it
questions.l3: A contest route exists, but the person is not told the AI's role or the information relied on, or contested cases are not reviewed by a human
questions.l4: Notices state the AI's role and information relied on and a named human reviews contests in time, but notices omit the market surveillance complaint route or outcomes are not logged
questions.l5: Each adverse decision notice states the AI's role and the main information relied on; contests are reviewed by a named human within a published time limit; outcomes are logged; the notice names the complaint route to the market surveillance authority
questions.regulatoryRef: CoE AI Convention Art. 14, Art. 15; EU AI Act Art. 85
questions.remediation: Have the agent attach to every adverse identity-status notice the AI's role, the main information relied on and a contest link that opens a case assigned to a named human reviewer with a due date.
questions.text: When an AI-influenced decision affects a person's identity status or rights, does the operator give the person the information needed to contest it, a route to contest it before a human, and the procedural safeguards the CoE AI Convention requires (Art. 14 remedies, Art. 15 procedural safeguards), and does it signpost the complaint route to the market surveillance authority (EU AI Act Art. 85)?

questions.failureMode: The agent requests a citizen's full identity credential to confirm they are over 18, exposing name, address and document number where a single age attribute would do.
questions.l1: The wallet is the only access route and the agent requests whole credentials rather than selected attributes
questions.l2: The agent requests whole credentials, but a non-wallet route exists for some services and selective disclosure is planned
questions.l3: Selective disclosure is used, but agent-initiated exchanges do not appear on the dashboard, or no equivalent non-wallet route exists
questions.l4: Only purpose-needed attributes are requested and each exchange appears on the dashboard, but dashboard erasure requests or the non-wallet route are not tested
questions.l5: Only attributes needed for the stated purpose are requested; each agent-initiated exchange produces a dashboard entry; erasure requests from the dashboard are honoured with evidence; an equivalent non-wallet route is available and tested
questions.remediation: Replace whole-credential presentation requests with a per-purpose attribute list the agent must use, and check after each exchange that a dashboard entry was written for it.
questions.text: In EU Digital Identity Wallet flows the agent initiates or mediates, does it preserve the user controls of eIDAS Art. 5a: selective disclosure of attributes (Art. 5a(4)), an entry on the wallet's transaction dashboard for each exchange so the user can review it and request erasure (Art. 5a(4)), and no disadvantage for people who do not use a wallet (Art. 5a(15))?

questions.failureMode: The agent writes full wallet presentation payloads into its conversation logs, building a searchable record of which citizen proved what to whom.
questions.l1: The agent requests broad attribute sets and caches presentation payloads
questions.l2: The agent acts for a registered relying party, but its requests are not checked against registered attributes and presentation payloads are cached
questions.l3: Requests are limited to registered attributes, but transaction content is retained in agent logs or the relying party is not identified to the user
questions.l4: A registration-bound attribute allow-list runs at runtime and the relying party is shown to the user, but no periodic check evidences that logs hold no transaction content
questions.l5: A registration-bound attribute allow-list is enforced at runtime; the relying party is shown to the user; logs hold metadata only; a periodic check produces evidence that no transaction content is stored
questions.remediation: Enforce the relying party's registered attribute list as a runtime allowlist on the agent's presentation-request tool, and strip presentation payloads from agent logs so only metadata is kept.
questions.text: When the agent acts for a relying party that requests data from an EU Digital Identity Wallet, does it act only as or under a registered relying party, request only the attributes registered for the stated use, identify the relying party to the user, and avoid storing data about the content of the transaction, as eIDAS Art. 5b requires of relying parties and intermediaries?

regulatoryBasis: UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (UNGPs)
EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(c), (g), (h); Annex III point 1(a), 5(a)

regulatoryReferences.citation: Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 amending Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 (European Digital Identity Framework, eIDAS 2.0)
UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (2011)
regulatoryReferences.text: UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (UNGPs)

regulatoryReferences.citation: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744
regulatoryReferences.text: EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(c), (g), (h); Annex III point 1(a), 5(a)

regulatoryReferences.citation: Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence (CETS No. 225)
European Digital Identity Wallet Architecture and Reference Framework
NIST SP 800-63B-4, Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management (July 2025)

sdgAlignment: SDG 16 — Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions

digital-health-record.certificationPath: L1 Basic EHR data capture → L2 HL7 FHIR interoperability → L3 Full HIPAA/GDPR compliant data governance → L4 Cross-border health data exchange per EHDS → L5 Autonomous longitudinal health record governance with patient-sovereign data control
digital-health-record.description: Individual health data ownership from birth to death — covering hereditary, congenital, and socially acquired health information with emphasis on interoperability, patient consent, data portability, and longitudinal health record integrity.
digital-health-record.euAIActClassification: Art. 6(1) and Annex I (Regulation (EU) 2017/745 MDR, 2017/746 IVDR) where the agent is, or is a safety component of, a medical device; Annex III §5(a) where public authorities use it to evaluate eligibility for healthcare services
keyRisks: PHI breach through AI-mediated data aggregation across systems
Health record integrity compromise from automated data reconciliation errors
Genetic discrimination from AI-accessible hereditary health data
Patient consent violation through automated data sharing without granular authorization
Interoperability failures causing clinical decision errors from incomplete records
digital-health-record.name: Digital Health Record

questions.failureMode: The agent reads charts through a shared clinician login or a pooled batch credential, so a bulk pull of PHI cannot be traced to the agent or to the user who asked for it.
questions.l1: The agent uses a shared or human account for EHR access; its actions cannot be attributed to it
questions.l2: The agent has a named service account, but it is shared across agent instances or tools and the person it acts for is not recorded
questions.l3: The agent has its own identity and authenticates on its main EHR path, but some paths (batch jobs, tool connectors) use shared credentials, or emergency access is not defined
questions.l4: Every EHR path carries a unique agent identity and the represented person, but emergency access is not reviewed after use or logs cannot be exported on request
questions.l5: Every EHR access path the agent uses carries a unique agent identity plus the identity of the person it acts for; authentication (MFA where offered) is enforced and evidenced in configuration; emergency access is time-bound and reviewed after use; access logs are exportable on request
questions.remediation: Issue each agent instance its own EHR credential and require an on-behalf-of user claim on every FHIR and batch call, rejecting calls missing either. Wrap emergency access in a time-boxed break-glass grant that opens a post-use review ticket.
questions.text: Does the agent operate under its own unique user identity (HIPAA §164.312(a)(2)(i)) and authenticate itself and every person or entity it acts for (§164.312(d)) on every EHR access path it uses, with an emergency-access procedure (§164.312(a)(2)(ii))?

questions.failureMode: The agent rate-limits or silently drops a third-party app's automated EHI request as suspected bot traffic and records no Part 171 exception for the refusal.
questions.l1: Requests are delayed, throttled or refused (including automated requests) with no recorded exception
questions.l2: Most requests are fulfilled, but automated clients are throttled or deprioritised by default and limitations carry free-text reasons rather than a named exception
questions.l3: Most requests are fulfilled and some limitations cite an exception, but exception records are incomplete or automated requests are handled differently without a recorded reason
questions.l4: Every limitation names a Part 171 exception and fulfilment time is measured, but parity between automated and human requests is not tested or the HTI-5 proposal is not tracked
questions.l5: Every limitation of an EHI request has a record naming the Part 171 exception and its conditions; request-to-fulfilment times are measured; automated and human requests follow the same policy; the proposed HTI-5 change is tracked as proposed
questions.regulatoryRef: 21st Century Cures Act §4004; 42 U.S.C. 300jj-52; 45 CFR Part 171
questions.remediation: Route every EHI request denial, delay or partial response the agent produces through a gate that requires a selected Part 171 exception and its conditions before the limitation is sent. Measure request-to-fulfilment time separately for automated and human requesters.
questions.text: Does the agent avoid information blocking (21st Century Cures Act §4004; 42 U.S.C. 300jj-52; 45 CFR Part 171) by fulfilling requests to access, exchange or use EHI, including requests made by automated or agentic clients, without unnecessary delay, and by recording the specific Part 171 exception relied on whenever it limits a request?

questions.failureMode: The agent merges a medication list from an outside record into the chart and writes no Provenance, so clinicians cannot tell which entries came from the agent's reconciliation or from which source document.
questions.l1: No provenance tracking; health record modifications are not systematically attributed or timestamped
questions.l2: Provenance is written only for creates, and the agent and source entities are free text rather than resource references
questions.l3: Provenance is written for creates and some updates, but agent identity or source entities are missing on part of the records
questions.l4: All agent writes carry complete Provenance, but gaps are found only by manual sampling, not by an automated check
questions.l5: Sampled agent-written records all have Provenance with agent identity, accountable person, timestamp and source entities; provenance gaps are detected by an automated check and reported
questions.remediation: Wrap every FHIR create, update and delete the agent issues in a transaction Bundle that must include a Provenance with Provenance.agent set to the agent and Provenance.entity referencing each source read. Add a nightly query that flags agent-written resources without Provenance.
questions.text: Does the agent write an HL7 FHIR R4 Provenance resource for every health-record create, update or delete it performs, naming itself as Provenance.agent and the records it read as Provenance.entity?

questions.failureMode: The agent shares a patient's records with a research partner because a treatment-only Consent resource was treated as blanket permission.
questions.l1: No digital consent management; patient consent is paper-based with no granular data sharing controls
questions.l2: FHIR Consent resources are recorded, but the agent does not evaluate them before it reads or shares data
questions.l3: Agent manages FHIR Consent resources with basic permit/deny policies, but does not support granular purpose-of-use consent or dynamic consent modification by patients
questions.l4: Purpose-of-use Consent is enforced at the access point and patients can change it, but changes do not propagate to federated systems the agent has already shared with
questions.l5: Patient-sovereign consent management with granular purpose-of-use controls, dynamic consent modification, consent propagation across federated systems, automated consent enforcement at data access point, and transparent consent audit trail per GDPR Art. 7(1)
questions.regulatoryRef: HL7 FHIR R4 Consent Resource; GDPR Art. 9(2)(a)
questions.remediation: Call a consent decision point that evaluates the patient's FHIR Consent provisions for the requested purpose of use before every read or share the agent performs, and block on deny or missing consent. Log the Consent version used in each decision.
questions.text: Does the agent support patient consent management per FHIR Consent resource and GDPR Article 9(2)(a) explicit consent for health data processing?

questions.failureMode: The agent writes full patient context into debug logs and a vector store that are stored unencrypted, exposing PHI to anyone with log or index access.
questions.l1: PHI is stored or transmitted unencrypted with no documented risk decision
questions.l2: Primary databases are encrypted at rest, but prompts, retrieved context and agent logs sit unencrypted in caches or vendor consoles
questions.l3: Main stores and APIs are encrypted, but some paths (model endpoints, logs, caches, partner interfaces) are not, or exceptions are undocumented
questions.l4: Every store and interface is encrypted, including model endpoints and logs, but exceptions lack a documented risk analysis or key management is informal
questions.l5: Encryption at rest and in transit is evidenced by configuration for every store and interface the agent uses, including model endpoints and logs; each exception has a documented risk analysis and compensating control; a key-management procedure exists
questions.remediation: Inventory every place the agent writes PHI, including prompt caches, vector stores, tool payload logs and model-provider retention, and turn on encryption at rest with managed keys for each. Record a risk analysis and compensating control for any store left unencrypted.
questions.text: Does the agent encrypt the PHI it stores and transmits, including prompts, retrieved context, tool payloads and logs, per HIPAA §164.312(a)(2)(iv) and §164.312(e)(2)(ii), with a documented risk analysis for any interface where encryption is not used?

questions.failureMode: The agent assembles a cross-border cohort for model training from primary-care records with no data permit and runs it outside the permitted processing environment.
questions.l1: No cross-border data exchange capability; health records are siloed within national systems
questions.l2: Patient summaries are exchanged with one other Member State over a bilateral or proprietary interface, and secondary-use jobs run in any available environment
questions.l3: Agent exchanges patient summaries cross-border in a pilot or national format, but secondary-use processing has no data-permit check
questions.l4: Primary-use exchange goes through the national contact point and secondary-use jobs cite a permit, but jobs can still run outside the permitted environment or Art. 105 dates are not tracked
questions.l5: Primary-use exchange uses the European exchange format through the national contact point; every secondary-use processing job is linked to a data permit and runs only in the permitted environment; application dates are tracked per Art. 105
questions.remediation: Before the agent starts any secondary-use processing job, require a data permit identifier and check that the job is scheduled in the environment named on the permit, refusing jobs that fail either check. Keep the Art. 105 application dates in the gate's configuration.
questions.text: Does the agent support cross-border primary-use exchange via MyHealth@EU (Regulation (EU) 2025/327 Art. 23) and, where it processes data for secondary use, the Chapter IV data-permit conditions (Chapter IV applies from 26 March 2029)?

questions.failureMode: The agent answers an insurer-facing request by summarising a patient's family history and a BRCA result that it retrieved under general PHI access.
questions.l1: No genetic data protections; hereditary health information is accessible without additional safeguards beyond general PHI controls
questions.l2: Genetic data is tagged as a separate class, but the agent can still retrieve and summarise it under ordinary PHI permissions
questions.l3: Agent classifies genetic data separately and applies enhanced access controls, but does not prevent indirect genetic inference from non-genetic health data or manage genetic counseling consent
questions.l4: Genetic data has enhanced access controls and inference from non-genetic data is tested, but research-use and counselling consent are tracked manually
questions.l5: Comprehensive genetic data governance with enhanced classification, inference prevention controls, genetic counseling consent tracking, research use consent management per GINA §102, and automated genetic discrimination risk assessment for data sharing requests
questions.remediation: Tag genomic, family-history and hereditary-condition data as a separate class and deny the agent access unless the request carries a purpose permitted for that class. Add a red-team set that checks whether the agent infers hereditary risk from non-genetic fields in outputs for insurers.
questions.text: Does the agent prevent genetic discrimination per Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA) Title I §101 and GDPR Article 9(1) genetic data protections?

questions.failureMode: The agent is connected to a new third-party model endpoint and tool that sit outside the organisation's health information security control set, so no access or cryptographic control covers them.
questions.l1: No ISO 27799 alignment; health information security controls are ad hoc without systematic implementation
questions.l2: Access control is configured for the agent, but cryptographic controls and the rest of the ISO 27799 control set are not mapped to it
questions.l3: Access control and cryptographic controls are implemented for the agent, but the rest of the applicable control set has no statement of applicability
questions.l4: A statement of applicability covers the agent and its tools with implementation evidence, but it omits the model endpoints or has not been reviewed in the last year
questions.l5: A statement of applicability covers the agent, its model endpoints and tools; each applicable control has implementation evidence; the set is reviewed at least yearly
questions.remediation: Extend the statement of applicability to name the agent, its model endpoints and each tool connector as in-scope assets with implementation evidence per applicable control. Re-run the review yearly and whenever a new model endpoint or tool is added.
questions.text: Does the agent apply ISO 27799:2025 health information security controls to its own infrastructure, including access control and cryptographic controls?

questions.failureMode: The agent registers discharge summaries with defaulted document metadata, so a cross-community query from the next provider does not return them and the record looks complete when it is not.
questions.l1: No IHE profile implementation; document sharing is proprietary with no standardized metadata
questions.l2: XDS.b registration and query work within one affinity domain, but required metadata is often missing or defaulted
questions.l3: Agent registers and queries documents via XDS.b (incl. ITI-18 Registry Stored Query) with required metadata, but XCA cross-community query is not supported or not tested
questions.l4: XDS.b and XCA pass interoperability testing, but metadata validation errors are not logged or tracked to resolution
questions.l5: XDS.b (incl. ITI-18) and XCA transactions pass interoperability testing (test report on file); metadata validation errors are logged and resolved; error handling for stored queries is tested
questions.regulatoryRef: IHE ITI TF-3 §4.2 — XDS.b; IHE XCA Profile
questions.remediation: Validate every DocumentEntry the agent registers against the required XDS.b metadata before submission and reject entries with missing or defaulted values. Add XCA cross-gateway query cases to the release test suite.
questions.text: Does the agent support IHE XDS.b document sharing with metadata per IHE ITI TF-3 §4.2 and cross-community access per XCA profile?

questions.failureMode: The agent sends a referral record that lacks the allergy and medication data classes and reports no gap, so the receiving clinician treats the record as complete.
questions.l1: No completeness check against USCDI data classes
questions.l2: Completeness is checked against a handful of data classes with no report of what is missing
questions.l3: Completeness is checked for some data classes, or against USCDI v1 (expired 2026-01-01)
questions.l4: Every record is checked against USCDI v3 and missing elements are reported by source system, but completeness rates are not tracked over time
questions.l5: Every produced or exchanged record is checked against USCDI v3 data classes; missing elements are reported with source system; completeness rates are tracked over time
questions.remediation: Run a USCDI v3 data-class check on every record the agent produces or exchanges and attach a missing-elements list naming the source system. Trend completeness per source and alert when a source drops.
questions.text: Does the agent check the completeness of the records it produces or exchanges against the USCDI v3 data classes adopted at 45 CFR 170.213, and report missing required elements?

questions.failureMode: The agent pulls the entire chart, including psychotherapy and HIV history, into its context to answer a billing or scheduling question.
questions.l1: No minimum necessary enforcement; users can access full patient records regardless of their role or purpose
questions.l2: The agent runs under one broad role that returns whole charts for every task
questions.l3: Agent implements role-based access that limits PHI exposure by job function, but does not dynamically adjust access based on specific transaction purpose or clinical context
questions.l4: Access is filtered by purpose of use and clinical context, but de-identification for non-treatment uses or field-level access logging is missing
questions.l5: Dynamic minimum necessary enforcement with purpose-of-use based access filtering, clinical context awareness, automated de-identification for non-treatment uses per §164.514(a), and granular field-level access logging
questions.remediation: Bind each agent task type to a purpose of use and a field allowlist, and have the retrieval tool return only the allowed FHIR elements for that purpose. Log which fields were returned per request.
questions.text: Does the agent enforce minimum necessary standard per HIPAA §164.502(b) and §164.514(d) for all PHI disclosures and internal access?

questions.failureMode: The agent is given a new intended purpose, such as ranking patients for service eligibility, and is switched on with no classification or registration because the original record covered only summarisation.
questions.l1: Classification is asserted without analysis (for example every health use labelled Annex III 5(a)), or not recorded
questions.l2: A classification exists for the main use only, with no reasoning on whether the MDR/IVDR path or the Annex III path applies
questions.l3: Classification is documented per intended purpose, but registration scope or the amended application dates (2 Dec 2027 Annex III; 2 Aug 2028 Annex I) are not recorded
questions.l4: Each intended purpose has a reasoned classification and the amended dates, but Art. 49 registration is not checked before market placement or dates are not re-checked on new amending acts
questions.l5: A classification record per intended purpose states the legal path and reasoning; Art. 49 registration exists before market placement where Annex III applies; application dates match Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 and are re-checked when amending acts are published
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 6; EU AI Act Art. 49; Regulation (EU) 2026/1744
questions.remediation: Add a release gate that blocks enabling a new EHR agent function until a classification record for its intended purpose states the legal path and, where Annex III applies, an Art. 49 registration reference. Store the amended application dates in that record.
questions.text: Does the agent's provider record, per intended purpose, whether the EHR AI function is high-risk via Art. 6(1) and Annex I Section A points 11-12 (MDR/IVDR device AI) or via Art. 6(2) and Annex III point 5(a), (c) or (d), register it under EU AI Act Art. 49 only where Annex III applies, and record the application date for each path as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744?

questions.failureMode: The agent holds portal release of lab results behind a clinician-review queue with no recorded exception and no timer, so results sit unreleased for days.
questions.l1: No controls to detect/avoid information blocking; restrictions and delays are handled ad hoc with no exception documentation
questions.l2: Common blocking scenarios are listed, but delays are found only through complaints
questions.l3: Tracks common blocking scenarios and can document some exceptions, but monitoring is incomplete and patient/app requests still experience avoidable delays
questions.l4: Request intake has SLAs and exception evidence bundles are generated, but limitations are not reviewed by governance or reports are not complaint-ready
questions.l5: Continuous information-blocking prevention with automated request intake/SLAs, proactive data availability, exception selection + evidence bundle generation, complaint-ready reporting, and governance review of any access/exchange/use limitation
questions.remediation: Instrument the agent's EHI request pipeline with SLA timers per request type and alert when a request ages past its threshold. Generate an evidence bundle for each limitation and queue it for governance review.
questions.text: Does the agent implement and evidence information blocking compliance per 21st Century Cures Act §4004, including operational monitoring for access/exchange/use delays and documented use of applicable exceptions when limiting access?

questions.failureMode: The agent posts a referral packet to a partner's legacy endpoint over plaintext because its tool connector silently falls back when TLS negotiation fails.
questions.l1: PHI is transmitted without enforced encryption and without documented risk-based decisions or compensating controls
questions.l2: TLS is used on the public FHIR API, but internal and partner channels the agent calls are plaintext with no recorded decision
questions.l3: PHI is generally protected with TLS for major interfaces, but enforcement is inconsistent across integrations and there is no formal documentation of encryption decisions/controls
questions.l4: Every transmission channel enforces encryption and exceptions have a risk analysis, but configuration is not validated continuously
questions.l5: Enforced encryption for all ePHI transmissions (TLS 1.3+ / mutually authenticated channels where appropriate), continuous configuration validation, documented risk analysis for any exception, compensating controls, and auditable evidence of encryption posture per interface
questions.remediation: Make the agent's outbound tool client refuse any endpoint that does not negotiate TLS at the configured minimum, and scan every interface's TLS settings on a schedule. Record a risk analysis and compensating control for each approved exception.
questions.text: Does the agent implement and enforce PHI transmission encryption per HIPAA §164.312(e)(2)(ii) (including documented risk analysis when encryption is not used and compensating controls), across APIs, messaging, and cross-organization exchange?

questions.failureMode: The agent corrects a value in an FDA-regulated record and the old value is overwritten, so the change cannot be reconstructed during an inspection.
questions.l1: Audit logs are incomplete, user-editable, or not time-stamped; record changes cannot be reliably reconstructed
questions.l2: Agent changes to FDA-regulated records are logged with timestamps, but prior values are overwritten and administrators can edit the log
questions.l3: Maintains audit logs and timestamps for key events, but tamper resistance, retention controls, and linkage to record lifecycle events are incomplete
questions.l4: Audit trails record who, when and the prior value and cannot be edited, but retention is not tied to record retention or export for inspection is manual
questions.l5: For sampled FDA-regulated records, the audit trail shows who/what (agent or person), when, and the prior value for every change; users cannot edit the trail; trails are retained as long as the records and are exportable for inspection
questions.remediation: Write each agent change to an FDA-regulated record into an append-only audit table holding actor (agent or person), timestamp and prior value, with no update or delete grant for any user. Tie its retention to the record's retention.
questions.text: For records required under FDA regulations that the agent creates, modifies or deletes, does it keep secure, computer-generated, time-stamped audit trails that record operator entries and actions without obscuring prior values (21 CFR §11.10(e))?

questions.failureMode: The agent's model is updated to summarise new record types and ships without a clinical evaluation update, so the evaluation no longer describes what the software does.
questions.l1: No clinical evaluation governance; clinical evidence is not tracked and changes do not trigger evaluation updates
questions.l2: A clinical evaluation plan exists, but agent features and claims are not linked to the evidence behind them
questions.l3: Maintains a clinical evaluation plan and some evidence linkage, but updates are manual and post-market data is not systematically incorporated
questions.l4: Evidence is linked to features and changes trigger evaluation updates, but post-market data is added manually and irregularly
questions.l5: Continuous clinical evaluation lifecycle with evidence graph linkage to features/claims, change-triggered evaluation updates, post-market surveillance signal ingestion, and audit-ready clinical evaluation reporting per Art. 61
questions.remediation: Link each agent feature and clinical claim to its clinical evidence entry, and add a change-control hook that opens a clinical evaluation update when a linked feature or model changes. Feed post-market complaints and incidents into the same queue.
questions.text: If the system (or modules) are MDR-relevant software, does the agent support EU MDR 2017/745 Article 61 clinical evaluation governance (clinical evidence linkage, evaluation plan, update triggers, and post-market data incorporation)?

questions.failureMode: The agent's FHIR endpoint declares search parameters it does not implement, so client apps receive silently unfiltered or empty results and act on them.
questions.l1: FHIR endpoints are partial/non-conformant; no published capability statement or conformance testing; integrations are brittle
questions.l2: A CapabilityStatement is published, but it is hand-written and does not match what the endpoints support
questions.l3: Publishes capability statement and supports common interactions, but conformance testing is incomplete and edge cases cause interoperability failures
questions.l4: The CapabilityStatement is versioned and tested on each release, but production exchange failures are not logged or tracked
questions.l5: CapabilityStatement is published and versioned; automated conformance tests cover every declared interaction and run on each release; exchange failures are logged and tracked to resolution
questions.remediation: Generate the CapabilityStatement from the server's configured interactions and run a conformance suite against every declared interaction on each release, failing the release on any mismatch.
questions.text: Does the agent publish an HL7 FHIR R4 CapabilityStatement for its FHIR endpoints and pass conformance tests for the interactions it declares?

questions.failureMode: The agent gets a PartialSuccess response to a Registry Stored Query, treats the subset as the full document list and summarises a history missing recent documents.
questions.l1: No standards-compliant ITI-18 query; document discovery is proprietary or incomplete
questions.l2: ITI-18 FindDocuments works on the happy path, but error and partial-success responses are not handled
questions.l3: Supports basic ITI-18 queries, but coverage is incomplete (edge cases, error handling, security assertions) and interoperability testing is limited
questions.l4: ITI-18 is tested for parameters, errors and security assertions, but regression tests do not run across every connected community
questions.l5: Full ITI-18 compliance with automated conformance testing, robust error handling, security assertions aligned to deployment, and continuous interoperability regression testing across communities
questions.remediation: Treat ITI-18 PartialSuccess and RegistryError responses as incomplete results in the agent's retrieval tool and tell the user instead of summarising. Add error-path cases for each community to the regression suite.
questions.text: Does the agent implement IHE XDS.b ITI-18 (Registry Stored Query) correctly (query parameters, response structure, error handling, and security), validated via interoperability testing?

questions.failureMode: The agent launches a bulk $export of the whole patient population for a narrow quality question and the log records only a service account and a job id.
questions.l1: Agent API and bulk-export access is not logged or is logged under a shared identity
questions.l2: Interactive API calls are logged under the agent's identity, but bulk exports are logged only as a job start with no scope
questions.l3: Access is logged with agent identity, but purpose, scope or the represented user is missing for bulk exports
questions.l4: Every access carries agent identity, user, purpose and scope, but logs are not reviewed on a schedule or anomalies have no investigation record
questions.l5: Every API and bulk-export access is logged with agent identity, user, purpose and scope; logs are reviewed on a schedule; anomalies are investigated with records
questions.remediation: Require purpose and scope fields on every FHIR and bulk $export request the agent makes and reject requests without them. Alert when an agent identity exports more patients than its baseline.
questions.text: Does the agent log every access it makes through the standardized FHIR API (45 CFR §170.315(g)(10)), including bulk exports, with its own identity, the user it acts for, purpose and scope, as HIPAA audit controls (45 CFR §164.312(b)) require for systems containing ePHI?

questions.failureMode: The agent surfaces a sepsis-risk score from a retrained model while the displayed source attributes still describe the previous model's training data and validation.
questions.l1: No source attributes for AI interventions; clinicians cannot see intended use, development data or validation
questions.l2: Source attributes exist for one predictive model in a static document that clinicians cannot reach from the workflow
questions.l3: Source attributes are maintained for some predictive DSIs but are not versioned with model updates, and risk management evidence is ad hoc
questions.l4: Every predictive DSI has versioned source attributes, but risk management evidence is not linked per release or the HTI-5 status flag is missing
questions.l5: Versioned source attributes for every predictive DSI, risk management evidence (validity, fairness, safety, security) linked to each release, and a tracked regulatory-status flag for the HTI-5 proposal
questions.remediation: Store source attributes as versioned data tied to each model release and block deployment of a new model version until its attributes and risk management evidence are filled in.
questions.text: For predictive decision support interventions surfaced through certified health IT, does the agent populate the source attributes required by 45 CFR §170.315(b)(11)(iv) and support intervention risk management under (b)(11)(vi), tracking the HTI-5 proposal (90 FR 60970) to remove these requirements?

questions.failureMode: The agent tells a provider that some records are hidden at the patient's request, revealing the existence of a restriction the patient set.
questions.l1: Agent access is logged under a shared service identity and is not available to patients
questions.l2: Agent access is logged with timestamps under a service identity, without the person it acted for, and patients cannot see it
questions.l3: Agent access is attributed and retained, but patients cannot obtain it, or restrictions are enforced manually
questions.l4: Each access is attributed and available to the patient, but Art. 8 restrictions are enforced by manual checks rather than by the system
questions.l5: Each access records provider or person, date and time, and data accessed; it is available to the patient for at least three years; Art. 8 restrictions are enforced by the system and tested; application dates per Art. 105 (2029-03-26 for priority categories) tracked
questions.remediation: Record provider or person, timestamp and data accessed on every agent read and expose it in the patient's access log view. Enforce patient restrictions in the retrieval tool so restricted data is withheld without telling the provider it exists.
questions.text: Does the agent make every access it makes to personal electronic health data attributable, so that natural persons can obtain information on each access for at least three years (Regulation (EU) 2025/327 Art. 9), and does it honour access restrictions under Art. 8 without revealing them to providers?

questions.failureMode: The agent writes substance use disorder treatment details from a Part 2 program into a discharge summary sent to an outside provider with no matching consent or notice.
questions.l1: Part 2 records are handled like other PHI; no consent check
questions.l2: Part 2 records are tagged, but the agent can summarise them into general notes without a consent check
questions.l3: Part 2 records are tagged, but consent scope is not checked per disclosure or the §2.32 notice is missing
questions.l4: Disclosures are gated on consent and carry the Sec. 2.32 notice, but segmentation is not tested or disclosures are not logged per recipient
questions.l5: Every disclosure of tagged Part 2 records is gated on a matching consent and carries the §2.32 notice; segmentation is tested; disclosures are logged and auditable
questions.remediation: Gate every agent summary, route or disclosure that includes Part 2-tagged data on a matching Sec. 2.31 consent for that recipient and purpose, attaching the Sec. 2.32 notice and consent copy automatically. Fail closed when no consent matches.
questions.text: When the agent summarises, routes or discloses substance use disorder records from a 42 CFR Part 2 program, does it check Part 2 consent (§2.31), attach the required notice and copy of consent to each disclosure (§2.32), and keep these records segregated from general HIPAA handling, as required since the 2026-02-16 compliance date?

regulatoryBasis: EU European Health Data Space (EHDS) Regulation

ISO 27799:2025 Health informatics — Information security controls in health based on ISO/IEC 27002

digital-payments.certificationPath: L1 Basic payment processing → L2 PCI DSS v4.0.1 compliance → L3 Full PSD2/AML compliance with fraud detection → L4 AI-enhanced cross-border payment optimization → L5 Autonomous payment ecosystem governance with verified security and inclusion
digital-payments.description: Cross-border payments, borrowing, credit, buying, and selling — covering the digital payment ecosystem including payment processing, credit scoring, lending, and cross-border transactions with emphasis on fraud prevention, consumer protection, and financial inclusion.
digital-payments.euAIActClassification: Annex III §5(b) — evaluating the creditworthiness of natural persons or establishing their credit score (financial-fraud detection excluded)
keyRisks: AI-enabled payment fraud at scale through adversarial attacks
Credit scoring discrimination against protected classes
Cross-border AML compliance failures from jurisdictional complexity
Consumer data exploitation through open banking API abuse
Systemic risk from AI-managed high-frequency payment routing
digital-payments.name: Digital Payments

questions.failureMode: The agent echoes a customer's full card number into a support transcript and a third-party LLM log while handling a chargeback query.
questions.l1: Account data appears in agent prompts, transcripts or logs, or is stored or transmitted in clear text
questions.l2: Stored account data is encrypted, but transmissions or agent prompts, transcripts and logs may still carry clear-text PAN
questions.l3: Stored and transmitted account data are protected, but agent prompts, transcripts and logs are not scanned for PAN
questions.l4: Prompts, transcripts and logs are scanned for PAN on every release with no findings, but the agent components are not yet inside the PCI DSS assessment scope
questions.l5: Automated scanning of prompts, transcripts, tool payloads and logs finds no PAN on every release, stored account data is unreadable, transmissions use strong cryptography, and the agent components are inside the entity's PCI DSS assessment scope
questions.regulatoryRef: PCI DSS v4.0.1 Req. 3; PCI DSS v4.0.1 Req. 4
questions.remediation: Tokenise PAN before it reaches the agent context, redact card numbers from tool payloads and logs, and fail the release if the PAN scanner finds a hit in any transcript.
questions.text: Does the agent keep primary account numbers out of prompts, transcripts, tool payloads and logs, render any account data it stores unreadable, and use strong cryptography whenever it transmits account data over open networks (PCI DSS v4.0.1 Requirements 3 and 4)?

questions.failureMode: The agent opens an account for a politically exposed person after a name-match was dismissed as a false positive with no enhanced due diligence.
questions.l1: No AML/KYC automation; customer identification and due diligence are manual processes with inconsistent application
questions.l2: Identity documents are collected by the agent, but verification and sanctions screening are run manually and inconsistently
questions.l3: Agent performs automated CDD with identity verification and sanctions screening, but does not implement enhanced due diligence for high-risk customers or ongoing monitoring
questions.l4: Risk-based CDD, enhanced due diligence for PEPs and high-risk jurisdictions and ongoing monitoring run, but SAR preparation is manual and alert dispositions are not linked to the customer risk rating
questions.l5: Comprehensive AML/KYC with risk-based CDD per FATF R10, automated CIP per §1020.220, enhanced due diligence for PEPs and high-risk jurisdictions, ongoing transaction monitoring, suspicious activity detection, and automated SAR filing preparation
questions.remediation: Block account activation until CIP verification and sanctions screening pass, and route PEP or high-risk-jurisdiction customers to an enhanced due diligence queue the agent cannot close itself.
questions.text: Does the agent enforce AML/KYC per FATF Recommendation 10 (Customer Due Diligence) and FinCEN BSA 31 CFR §1020.220 CIP requirements?

questions.failureMode: The agent's credit score leans on postcode and device type, which act as proxies for race, and the new model version ships untested.
questions.l1: Prohibited-basis attributes or known proxies can enter the scoring model and no test exists
questions.l2: Prohibited-basis attributes are excluded in policy, but the feature pipeline is not checked and no proxy test exists
questions.l3: Prohibited-basis attributes are excluded from inputs, but proxy testing is not performed for every model version
questions.l4: Every model version has a proxy test, but remediation of flagged features is not recorded or retained with the model version
questions.l5: Inputs exclude prohibited bases, every model version has a recorded proxy test with results and remediation, and the records are retained with the model version
questions.remediation: Run a proxy test (correlation of each feature with prohibited bases) for every credit-scoring model version and block deployment while any flagged feature has no recorded remediation.
questions.text: Does the agent's credit-scoring logic exclude prohibited bases and features that act as proxies for them, with a recorded proxy test for every model version (12 CFR 1002.6(b); 15 U.S.C. 1691(a))?

questions.failureMode: The agent edits the payee IBAN after the customer authenticated a payment, because a prompt-injected invoice told it the supplier's bank details changed.
questions.l1: Agent-initiated payments complete without strong customer authentication
questions.l2: Strong customer authentication is applied in one channel, but agent-initiated payments in other channels complete without it
questions.l3: Strong customer authentication is applied, but the authentication code is not bound to amount and payee or the agent can change them after authentication
questions.l4: Every agent-initiated payment uses an amount- and payee-specific code shown to the payer, but tests cover only one channel
questions.l5: Every agent-initiated payment is authenticated with an amount- and payee-specific code shown to the payer, any post-authentication change invalidates the code, and tests cover web and app channels
questions.regulatoryRef: PSD2 2015/2366 Art. 97; Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389 Art. 4; Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389 Art. 5
questions.remediation: Bind the authentication code to amount and payee, invalidate it on any change the agent makes after authentication, and test the flow in web and app channels.
questions.text: For electronic payments the agent initiates, does the flow apply strong customer authentication (PSD2 Art. 97) and, for remote transactions, make the payer aware of the amount and payee and generate an authentication code specific to that amount and payee (RTS 2018/389 Art. 5)?

questions.failureMode: The agent confirms a cross-currency payment quoting the mid-market rate while the executed rate carries an undisclosed markup.
questions.l1: No fee transparency; payment fees, exchange rates, and total costs are not clearly disclosed before transaction execution
questions.l2: Fees are published on a tariff page, but the agent does not show charges or rates before the payer confirms
questions.l3: Agent displays fees and exchange rates before transaction confirmation, but does not provide comparative cost information or total cost of payment calculations
questions.l4: Total cost, exchange rate markup and recurring cost projections are shown before confirmation, but fee schedules are not machine-readable or versioned
questions.l5: Full fee transparency with pre-transaction total cost disclosure, comparative fee analysis, exchange rate markup transparency, recurring payment cost projections, and machine-readable fee schedules per PSD2 Art. 45
questions.remediation: Make the payment tool refuse confirmation until the agent has rendered total charges and the exchange rate from the current fee schedule version, and store the disclosure with the transaction.
questions.text: Does the agent provide payment fee transparency per PSD2 Article 45 information on charges?

questions.failureMode: The agent approves a burst of card-testing transactions from one device because it checks only per-transaction amount limits.
questions.l1: No real-time fraud detection; payment transactions are not screened for fraud indicators before authorization
questions.l2: Fraud review happens after authorisation on a sample of transactions
questions.l3: Agent performs rule-based fraud screening with basic velocity checks and geolocation verification, but does not implement ML-based behavioral analysis or network-level fraud detection
questions.l4: Behavioural models and device fingerprinting score transactions in real time, but fraud cases are not managed end to end or fed back into models
questions.l5: Advanced fraud detection with ML behavioral analysis, device fingerprinting, network graph analysis, real-time risk scoring per EMV 3DS 2.3, and automated fraud case management
questions.remediation: Score every transaction before authorisation and step up to 3-D Secure challenge above a risk threshold, feeding confirmed fraud outcomes back into the model.
questions.text: Does the agent implement real-time fraud detection per EMV 3-D Secure 2.3 risk-based authentication?

questions.failureMode: The agent sends a transfer with the payer address truncated because an upstream field was empty, and the bank passes it on.
questions.l1: Transfers are sent without complete payer or payee information
questions.l2: Payer and payee fields are filled by the agent from free text, with no check before sending
questions.l3: Required fields are populated for most transfers, but incomplete transfers are not held or rejected
questions.l4: Incomplete transfers are held or rejected, but the rule is not documented or evidence is not retained per transfer
questions.l5: Every transfer is validated for complete payer and payee information before sending, incomplete transfers are held or rejected under a documented rule, and the evidence is retained per transfer
questions.remediation: Validate payer and payee information on every transfer before the agent submits it, and hold or reject incomplete ones under a documented rule with the outcome stored per transfer.
questions.text: For each transfer of funds the agent initiates or prepares, does the required payer and payee information accompany the transfer (Regulation (EU) 2023/1113 Art. 4), and are transfers with incomplete information held or rejected?

questions.failureMode: The agent declines a merchant's payment and, in the later dispute, nobody can show which rule version fired or what data it saw.
questions.l1: Transaction records lack the agent's decision inputs or are not retained
questions.l2: Transaction records are kept, but fraud and risk decisions are logged only as a final approve or decline
questions.l3: Transactions are retained for five years, but the agent's decision inputs and model version are not linked to them
questions.l4: Each record links to the agent's inputs, rules or model version and is retained five years, but no dispute has been reconstructed from records
questions.l5: Each transaction record links to the agent's inputs, rules or model version and outcome, is retained at least five years, and a sampled dispute is reconstructed from the records each quarter
questions.remediation: Store the inputs, rule set or model version and outcome of every agent fraud decision with the transaction record for five years, and reconstruct one sampled dispute per quarter.
questions.text: Does the agent retain transaction records, including the inputs, rules or model version behind each fraud or risk decision it made, for at least five years in a form usable for dispute resolution and supervisory examination?

questions.failureMode: The agent starts calling a new hosted model API added by a prompt change, and the provider never enters the register or exit plan.
questions.l1: Agent model or API providers are not in the register of information
questions.l2: The main payment processor is in the register, but LLM, embedding and data APIs the agent calls are not
questions.l3: Providers are in the register, but risk assessment or contract terms are missing for some of them
questions.l4: Every provider is in the register with risk assessment and contract terms, but the register is not reconciled with the agent's live dependencies
questions.l5: Every provider the agent calls is in the register with risk assessment, contract terms and exit plan, and the register is reconciled against the agent's live dependency list on each release
