questions.text: When the agent tenders, routes or consolidates freight, does it verify hazardous-materials classification, shipping-paper content and emergency-response information against 49 CFR Part 172 (and the IMDG Code for sea legs) and stop non-conforming shipments before pickup?

questions.failureMode: The agent ranks pickers by rate and moves low scorers to harder zones, triggering discipline with no human review.
questions.l1: Task allocation and performance scoring run without named human oversight, log retention or any notice to workers
questions.l2: Supervisors can view allocations, but no one is named to oversee them and logs rotate within weeks.
questions.l3: Supervisors can review and override allocations and logs are kept, but retention is not tied to the six-month minimum and workers were not formally informed before deployment
questions.l4: Named overseers can intervene and logs are retained for six months, but workers and their representatives were not informed before use.
questions.l5: Named, trained overseers can intervene in allocation and evaluation, logs are retained for at least six months under a documented policy, workers' representatives and affected workers were informed before use, and the Annex III obligations are tracked against their application date
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Annex III §4(b); EU AI Act Art. 26(2), (6), (7)
questions.remediation: Log every task allocation and performance score the agent produces with its inputs for at least six months, and route score-based discipline flags to a named overseer.
questions.text: Where the agent allocates warehouse or driver tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits, or monitors and evaluates worker performance (high-risk under EU AI Act Annex III §4(b)), does the deployer assign competent human oversight (Art. 26(2)), keep the system's logs for at least six months (Art. 26(6)), and inform workers' representatives and affected workers before use (Art. 26(7))?

questions.failureMode: The agent reroutes around a ransomware-hit WMS and keeps fulfilling as if it were an outage, so the significant incident is never reported.
questions.l1: Incidents affecting TMS, WMS or carrier integrations are handled ad hoc with no reporting clock
questions.l2: TMS and WMS incidents are ticketed without an awareness time.
questions.l3: Incidents are logged with timestamps and a reporting contact, but significance assessment and the 24-hour and 72-hour deadlines are tracked manually
questions.l4: Significance and both deadlines are tracked automatically, but drafts are written by hand or affected service recipients are not notified.
questions.l5: Significance is assessed against documented criteria, the 24-hour early warning and 72-hour notification are drafted from incident evidence and tracked to submission, and recipients of affected services are notified where required
questions.remediation: Start the 24-hour and 72-hour clocks when the agent detects a TMS, WMS or carrier-integration incident, and draft both submissions from the incident record.
questions.text: For logistics operators in scope of NIS2, does the agent support significant-incident reporting to the CSIRT or competent authority with an early warning within 24 hours and an incident notification within 72 hours of becoming aware (NIS2 Art. 23(4))?

questions.failureMode: The agent sends AMRs through a pedestrian aisle outside their assessed movement space to meet a carrier cut-off time.
questions.l1: Agent instructions to machinery are outside any safety assessment, and no decision or version records are kept.
questions.l2: The robot vendor's safety assessment exists, but it does not cover the agent's task instructions.
questions.l3: The movement envelope is enforced, but decision-data or software-version retention is partial, or the stop/correction path is untested.
questions.l4: The envelope is enforced and tested and retention meets the stated periods, but the supervisory function or correction path is not tested on schedule.
questions.l5: The task and movement envelope is enforced and tested, safety-decision data are kept one year and the software-version trace five years, the correction/stop path and the supervisory function are tested with records.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230 Annex III 1.2.1; EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230 Annex III 3.2.4; ISO 3691-4:2023
questions.remediation: Check each AMR or AGV mission the agent issues against the defined task and movement space before dispatch, and archive the safety-decision data with the software version.
questions.text: Where the agent directs autonomous mobile robots, AGVs or other machinery with autonomous or self-evolving control, does the deployment evidence the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 Annex III requirements that apply from 20 January 2027: no actions beyond the defined task and movement space, safety-decision data retained for one year, a trace of safety-software versions retained for five years, correction possible at all times (EHSR 1.2.1), and a supervisory function for autonomous mobile machinery (EHSR 3.2.4)?

questions.failureMode: The agent drops upstream supplier and origin fields when consolidating shipments, so the operator cannot answer an authority's information request.
questions.l1: Shipment records do not keep supplier or origin data beyond the immediate shipper
questions.l2: Supplier names are recorded for direct shippers only, without origin.
questions.l3: Origin and supplier fields are captured for some lanes, but evidence is incomplete and cannot be assembled per product on request
questions.l4: Supplier, origin and route evidence is retained per shipment, but it cannot yet be assembled per product on request.
questions.l5: Supplier, origin and route evidence is retained per product and shipment, can be assembled on request, and the 14 December 2027 application date is tracked in the compliance plan
questions.remediation: Capture supplier and origin fields at booking on every lane, and have the agent assemble a per-product evidence dossier on demand.
questions.text: Does the agent retain supplier, origin and route evidence that lets the operator respond to information requests and decisions under the EU Forced Labour Regulation (EU) 2024/3015, which applies from 14 December 2027?

questions.failureMode: The agent forwards consignee addresses and proof-of-delivery photos to a sub-carrier with no processor contract or authorisation.
questions.l1: Consignee data flows to partners with no processor contracts
questions.l2: Processor contracts are planned, but consignee data are shared with partners by default.
questions.l3: Main partners have processor contracts, but sub-carriers and sub-processors are not tracked
questions.l4: Every processor and sub-processor has an Art. 28 contract and authorisation, but data flows are not logged per partner.
questions.l5: Agent only routes personal data to partners with a valid Article 28 contract, sub-processors are authorised and listed, and data flows are logged per partner
questions.remediation: Check the partner's Art. 28 contract status before the agent sends consignee names, addresses or delivery photos, and block the transfer when none is on file.
questions.text: When the agent shares consignee personal data (names, addresses, delivery photos, signatures) with carriers, 3PLs or other processors, is each processor bound by a contract with the terms GDPR Article 28(3) requires, and is every sub-processor authorised under Article 28(2)?

questions.failureMode: The agent emails a consignment note with consignee data to an address claiming to be an inspection authority, bypassing authenticated eFTI access.
questions.l1: Regulatory freight information exists only on paper or as unstructured files.
questions.l2: Freight documents are scanned to PDF and emailed to authorities on request.
questions.l3: The eFTI data set is mapped, but the platform is not certified or access logging is incomplete.
questions.l4: The eFTI platform is used with authenticated access and the common data set, but log archiving or the paper fallback is not documented.
questions.l5: A certified platform is used, its access and processing logs are archived for the required period, the common data set is covered, and the fallback to paper documents is documented.
questions.remediation: Have the agent make regulatory freight information available only through the eFTI platform with authenticated access, and archive its access and processing logs.
questions.text: When the agent makes regulatory freight information available to authorities electronically, does it use a certified eFTI platform (Regulation (EU) 2020/1056 Art. 4(2)) with authenticated access (Art. 9(1)(f)), operation logs recorded and archived (Art. 9(1)(g), (i)), and data protected against corruption and theft (Art. 9(1)(j)), ready for authorities' mandatory acceptance from 9 July 2027?

regulatoryReferences.citation: ISO 28000:2022 Security and resilience — Security management systems (with Amd 1:2024)
NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1 (update 1, 2024-11-01) Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management Practices

future-of-work.certificationPath: L1 Basic workforce management → L2 Labor law compliance automation → L3 Full EU Platform Work Directive compliance → L4 Algorithmic management transparency with worker rights → L5 Autonomous fair work governance with verified equity outcomes
future-of-work.description: Income generation, intellectual property, and individual/collective work — covering the evolving labor landscape including gig economy, remote work, algorithmic management, and worker data rights with emphasis on fair labor practices and equitable opportunity.
future-of-work.euAIActClassification: Annex III §4 — employment, workers' management and access to self-employment (recruitment, task allocation, performance monitoring)
keyRisks: Algorithmic wage discrimination across demographics
Worker misclassification through AI-managed gig platforms
Surveillance overreach in AI-monitored remote work
Skill obsolescence acceleration from AI automation without reskilling
Collective bargaining undermining through algorithmic management
future-of-work.name: Future of Work

questions.failureMode: The agent ranks candidates with a new model version whose selection rate for one group falls below four-fifths of the highest group, and nobody sees it until hiring is complete.
questions.l1: No selection-rate data by group is recorded for decisions the agent influences
questions.l2: Selection rates by group are computed once for a launch or pilot, but are not recomputed per model version and shortfalls are not logged
questions.l3: Selection rates by group are computed at least annually and four-fifths shortfalls are logged, but shortfalls have no recorded investigation or outcome
questions.l4: Selection rates are computed per model version and cohort and every shortfall is investigated, but investigation outcomes are not linked to the model version or retained for review
questions.l5: Selection rates by group are computed for every model version and decision cohort; every four-fifths shortfall has a recorded investigation with its outcome (validity evidence, change made, or tool withdrawn), retained for review
questions.remediation: Compute group selection rates for every screening model version and decision cohort, and block promotion of a version until each four-fifths shortfall has a recorded investigation outcome.
questions.text: Before outputs of the agent are used to screen, rank or select candidates or to allocate work, are selection rates compared across race, sex and ethnic groups using the four-fifths rule of 29 CFR 1607.4(D), with each shortfall investigated and recorded?

questions.failureMode: The agent onboards couriers as self-employed from a template while it sets their pay, allocates their jobs and sanctions them, with no record of the control it exercises.
questions.l1: Status is assigned by the agent or a contract template with no record of direction-and-control facts
questions.l2: Onboarding captures some direction-and-control facts in free text, but status is still set by the contract template
questions.l3: Direction-and-control facts are recorded at onboarding, but status determinations are not reviewed by a human or are not retained per person
questions.l4: Every status determination is taken and recorded by a named human with the facts considered, but changes to agent-driven pay, allocation or sanction controls do not trigger re-assessment
questions.l5: For every person the facts considered, the status outcome, the human decision-maker and the date are recorded, and changes to agent-driven controls (pay setting, allocation, ratings, sanctions) trigger a recorded re-assessment
questions.remediation: Record the direction-and-control facts per person at onboarding, route the status decision to a named human, and open a re-assessment task whenever the agent's pay-setting, allocation, rating or sanction rules change.
questions.text: When the agent onboards or manages persons performing platform work, does it record the facts indicating direction and control that bear on the Art. 5 legal presumption of an employment relationship, and is each status determination taken and recorded by a human?

questions.failureMode: The agent starts using a new ranking parameter for job allocation while workers and their representatives still hold a notice describing the previous system.
questions.l1: No information is given about the automated systems the agent operates
questions.l2: Information on the automated systems exists only in internal documentation and is given to workers or representatives on request
questions.l3: A static notice exists, but it is not tied to the deployed system versions or is not re-issued on change
questions.l4: Information is generated from the live system inventory and delivered before use, but re-issue on material change is manual and delivery evidence is incomplete
questions.l5: The Art. 9 information is generated from the live system inventory, delivered before use with delivery evidence, and re-issued with a version reference on every material change
questions.remediation: Generate the Art. 9 notice from the deployed system inventory (systems, data categories, aims, decision types, main parameters) and make a material version change fail release until the notice is re-issued with delivery evidence.
questions.text: Does the platform give persons performing platform work, their representatives and, on request, competent authorities the Art. 9 information on each automated monitoring or decision system the agent operates (systems in use, data categories, aims, decision types, main parameters), before use and on every material change?

questions.failureMode: The agent ingests in-app chat sentiment and off-shift location pings into a worker risk score that predicts likely organising activity.
questions.l1: No restriction on these data categories
questions.l2: Prohibited categories are listed in policy and some obvious fields are removed manually from feature pipelines
questions.l3: A written policy prohibits these categories, but enforcement is manual and untested
questions.l4: Feature allow-lists exclude the Art. 7(1) categories and off-shift collection is blocked, but no automated release test proves the categories are absent
questions.l5: Input and feature allow-lists exclude the Art. 7(1) categories, off-shift collection is blocked, and automated tests run on every release prove none of the categories is ingested
questions.remediation: Enforce an input and feature allow-list that excludes emotional state, private conversations, off-shift data and union-activity predictors, and add a release test that fails if any such field reaches the agent.
questions.text: Does the agent technically prevent processing of personal data on the emotional or psychological state of persons performing platform work, their private conversations, data collected while they are not performing platform work, and data used to predict the exercise of fundamental rights such as union activity?

questions.failureMode: The agent lowers job allocation for workers who post in an organising channel because it treats their reduced acceptance rate as a performance signal.
questions.l1: No collective bargaining support; algorithmic management does not accommodate worker organization or collective negotiation
questions.l2: The agent does not block worker communication channels, but provides no aggregate data or consultation route for representatives
questions.l3: Agent does not interfere with worker communication and provides aggregate workforce data for collective bargaining, but does not proactively facilitate worker representation
questions.l4: Aggregate workforce data is provided and representatives are consulted on algorithmic management changes, but non-interference is not verified by tests or monitoring
questions.l5: Full collective bargaining support with worker communication channel protection, aggregate data provision for negotiations, algorithmic management consultation mechanisms, works council integration, and non-interference verification per ILO C087/C098
questions.regulatoryRef: ILO Convention C087 Art. 2; C098 Art. 1-4
questions.remediation: Add a non-interference test that proves the agent never downranks, deactivates or reroutes workers based on union or channel activity, and log each algorithmic-management change consulted with representatives.
questions.text: Does the agent support collective bargaining and worker representation per ILO Convention C087 freedom of association and C098 right to organize?

questions.failureMode: The agent absorbs a whole claims-handling task family and the affected staff learn of it from a headcount plan with no reskilling route.
questions.l1: No automation impact assessment; AI deployment decisions do not consider workforce displacement or reskilling needs
questions.l2: Roles affected by automation are listed for a project, but no reskilling opportunity is identified for them
questions.l3: Agent tracks roles affected by automation and identifies reskilling opportunities, but does not implement systematic transition support or measure reskilling effectiveness
questions.l4: Displacement forecasts and personalised reskilling pathways exist for affected roles, but reskilling effectiveness is not measured against redeployment outcomes
questions.l5: Comprehensive automation impact management with displacement forecasting, personalized reskilling pathway generation, transition support coordination, skills gap analysis, reskilling effectiveness measurement, and just transition planning per ILO Centenary Declaration
questions.regulatoryRef: WEF Future of Jobs Framework; ILO Centenary Declaration (2019)
questions.remediation: Require an automation impact assessment naming affected roles before the agent takes over a task family, and track each affected worker's reskilling pathway to a redeployment or exit outcome.
questions.text: Does the agent assess automation impact on workforce and support reskilling per WEF Future of Jobs Framework and ILO Centenary Declaration?

questions.failureMode: The agent offers a surge shift to a driver who logged off eight hours earlier, cutting the daily rest period to win a delivery SLA.
questions.l1: No working time compliance; algorithmic scheduling does not enforce maximum working hours or minimum rest periods
questions.l2: Working hours are visible in the scheduling system, but limits are not checked by the agent
questions.l3: Agent tracks working hours and flags potential violations of daily/weekly limits, but does not prevent algorithmic scheduling that circumvents rest period requirements
questions.l4: Scheduling blocks shifts that breach daily rest, breaks, weekly rest and the weekly maximum, but hours worked across multiple apps or accounts are not aggregated
questions.l5: Full working time compliance with automated scheduling constraints per Art. 3 (11h daily rest), Art. 4 (rest breaks), Art. 5 (weekly rest), Art. 6 (48h weekly maximum), night work protections per Art. 8, and transparent working time reporting
questions.remediation: Encode the daily rest, break, weekly rest, weekly maximum and night-work limits as hard constraints in the agent's shift allocator, rejecting any offer that would breach them.
questions.text: Does the agent manage working time and rest period compliance per EU Working Time Directive 2003/88/EC Article 3-6 for algorithmically managed workers?

questions.failureMode: The agent rejects a candidate and, when the candidate challenges it, the logs have rotated so no one can show which inputs or model produced the rejection.
questions.l1: Logs are not retained or cannot be linked to individual decisions
questions.l2: Some decision logs exist, but they rotate before six months or are lost on redeploy
questions.l3: Logs are retained for at least six months, but cannot be linked to a specific decision, input set and model version
questions.l4: Logs are retained and each decision links to inputs, model version and reviewer, but reconstruction has never been tested on a sampled decision
questions.l5: Logs are retained for at least six months (or longer where another law requires), each decision links to its inputs, model version and human reviewer, and a sampled reconstruction is tested each quarter
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 26(6); EU AI Act Art. 12
questions.remediation: Write a decision record per worker or candidate decision with input hash, model version and human reviewer, retain it at least six months, and reconstruct a sampled decision each quarter.
questions.text: Does the deployer retain the logs automatically generated by the employment AI system for at least six months, linked to each decision that affects a worker or candidate, so that any individual decision can be reconstructed?

questions.failureMode: The agent auto-suspends a worker's account after a fraud score crosses a threshold, cutting off income with no human decision.
questions.l1: The agent can restrict, suspend or terminate without a human decision
questions.l2: Human approval is configured for account terminations, but the approval step can be skipped by an admin flag
questions.l3: A human approves terminations, but restrictions, suspensions or other detrimental decisions can take effect on the agent's output alone
questions.l4: A technical gate blocks every detrimental decision until a named human records reasons, but bypass attempts are not logged or tested
questions.l5: A technical gate blocks every detrimental decision until a named human records the decision and reasons; gate bypass attempts are logged and tested on each release
questions.remediation: Put a hard gate in front of the suspend, restrict and deactivate tools so they return pending until a named human records the decision and reasons, and test that the agent cannot call them directly.
questions.text: Before any decision to restrict, suspend or terminate the contractual relationship or account of a person performing platform work, or any decision of equivalent detriment, takes effect, is it taken by a named human rather than by the agent?

questions.failureMode: The agent scores NYC applicants with a resume-ranking tool whose bias audit has lapsed and sends no notice that an AEDT is in use.
questions.l1: No NYC LL144 support: no independent bias audit workflow, no audit summary publication, and no candidate/employee notice process for AEDT use
questions.l2: Internal bias testing is run once, with no independent auditor and no candidate notice
questions.l3: Performs some bias testing and can generate an internal report, but independence/audit cadence is unclear and notices/public postings are incomplete or manual
questions.l4: An independent bias audit runs annually and the summary is published, but candidate and employee notices are sent manually and delivery is not tracked
questions.l5: Full NYC LL144 readiness: independent bias audit support (metrics, protected classes, selection rates), annual scheduling and evidence retention, public audit-summary generation, and automated compliant notice delivery and tracking for candidates/employees
questions.regulatoryRef: NYC Local Law 144 (NYC Admin Code §20-870 et seq.)
questions.remediation: Block AEDT scoring for NYC candidates unless a current independent bias audit is on file and the notice has been delivered, and log each delivery against the candidate record.
questions.text: Does the agent support NYC Local Law 144 compliance for Automated Employment Decision Tools (AEDTs), including: (1) annual independent bias audit and publication of a bias audit summary, and (2) required candidate/employee notices about AEDT use, job qualifications assessed, and access to audit information, per NYC Admin Code §20-870 et seq.?

questions.failureMode: The agent analyses a recorded interview for facial expressions before the applicant consented, and keeps a vendor copy after a deletion request.
questions.l1: No notice, explanation or consent before AI analysis of interviews
questions.l2: A generic AI-use notice is shown in the application portal, but consent is not captured per applicant before analysis
questions.l3: Notice and consent are captured, but explanations are generic or deletion on request is not evidenced
questions.l4: Notice, explanation and consent are recorded per applicant, but deletion requests are tracked manually and copies in vendor storage are not covered
questions.l5: Notice, explanation and consent are recorded per applicant before analysis, and each deletion request is fulfilled with a dated deletion record covering all copies
questions.remediation: Hold each video interview out of the analysis queue until the applicant's notice, explanation and consent are recorded, and run deletion requests against every storage location including vendor copies.
questions.text: If the agent analyses video interviews, does it give written notice that AI will be used, explain how the AI works and which characteristics it evaluates, obtain consent before analysis, and delete the video and copies on the applicant's request?

questions.failureMode: The agent screens out an applicant with a speech impairment because a timed voice assessment scored them low, with no offer of an alternative format.
questions.l1: No accommodation route; applicants are scored only by the automated assessment
questions.l2: An accommodation contact address is listed, but applicants are scored before any request is handled
questions.l3: An accommodation request route exists, but screen-out criteria have no recorded job-relatedness evidence
questions.l4: Accommodation is offered before scoring and job-relatedness evidence exists per criterion, but evidence is not re-reviewed when the model changes
questions.l5: Accommodation is offered before scoring with request and outcome records, and each screen-out criterion has recorded job-relatedness evidence reviewed on every model change
questions.remediation: Offer an accommodation choice (alternative format or human assessment) before the agent scores an applicant, and refuse to deploy a screen-out criterion without a recorded job-relatedness review.
questions.text: Does the agent's assessment workflow offer applicants with disabilities a reasonable-accommodation route (alternative format or human assessment) before scoring, and is every criterion that screens out individuals with disabilities shown to be job-related and consistent with business necessity?

questions.failureMode: The agent rolls out a new rating penalty while open grievances about the previous one sit unconnected to the change.
questions.l1: No OECD due diligence loop: no structured labor-impact assessment, no worker consultation evidence, and grievances/remediation are not tracked
questions.l2: Labour impacts are discussed informally, and grievances arrive by email with no case record
questions.l3: Performs periodic assessments and tracks some grievances, but consultation and remediation evidence is incomplete and not connected to algorithmic decisions
questions.l4: Impact assessments, worker consultation and grievance cases are recorded and linked to algorithmic changes, but mitigation effectiveness is not measured or reported
questions.l5: Full OECD §V operationalization with continuous impact due diligence, documented worker engagement, grievance and remediation case management, and auditable reporting of mitigation effectiveness tied to algorithmic-management changes
questions.remediation: Link every worker grievance case to the algorithmic-management change it concerns, and require a recorded impact review with worker consultation before such a change ships.
questions.text: Does the agent support OECD MNE Guidelines 2023 §V by enabling labor-rights due diligence for algorithmic management (impact identification, prevention/mitigation, worker consultation/engagement, grievance intake, and remediation tracking), with evidence outputs suitable for internal/external accountability?

questions.failureMode: The agent's video-interview scoring is switched on for Illinois applicants by a global flag before the location's consent duties are met.
questions.l1: No applicability matrix; feature rollout does not account for jurisdiction-specific compliance triggers
questions.l2: Teams know of some location-specific duties, but no matrix exists and rollout is not checked
questions.l3: Maintains a manual policy memo, but gating and evidence retention are inconsistent across teams and releases
questions.l4: A jurisdiction matrix gates rollout, but evidence of completed notice, audit and consent duties is stored per team and not bundled per release
questions.l5: Automated scope gating with jurisdiction/role mapping, rollout checks, and evidence bundles demonstrating completion of all location-specific duties prior to deployment
questions.regulatoryRef: Jurisdictional scope gating for employment AI laws
questions.remediation: Map each employment AI feature to the jurisdictions where it runs and make the rollout pipeline fail for a location until its notice, audit or consent evidence is attached.
questions.text: Does the program maintain a jurisdictional applicability matrix for employment AI features (e.g., AEDT use in NYC; AI video interview analysis in Illinois), and gate feature rollout on completion of location-specific notice/audit/consent requirements with evidence retention?

questions.failureMode: The agent starts monitoring warehouse pick rates at a new site before workers or their representatives were told it would.
questions.l1: Workers and their representatives are not informed before workplace AI is deployed
questions.l2: Workers are told about workplace AI informally through managers, with no record of who was told
questions.l3: A generic notice is published, but it is not tied to specific systems, sites or go-live dates
questions.l4: Notices are recorded per system and site before go-live, but recipient lists for workers' representatives are incomplete
questions.l5: Go-live is gated on a recorded notice to workers' representatives and affected workers for each system and site, with the notice text, date and recipients retained
questions.remediation: Gate go-live of each high-risk workplace AI system per site on a recorded notice to workers' representatives and affected workers, storing the text, date and recipients.
questions.text: Before a high-risk AI system is put into service or used at the workplace, does the deployer inform workers' representatives and the affected workers that they will be subject to it, as EU AI Act Article 26(7) requires, and keep evidence of the notice?

questions.failureMode: The agent answers a worker's request to review a pay deduction with a canned chatbot message and the request is never escalated.
questions.l1: No review channel for decisions taken or supported by the agent
questions.l2: Review requests are accepted by chat, but replies are verbal or templated and no clock is kept
questions.l3: Review requests are logged, but replies are not written and substantiated or the two-week limits are not tracked
questions.l4: Written substantiated replies are sent and timed, but rectification deadlines are not tracked or breaches are not reported
questions.l5: Every review request has a timestamped written reply within two weeks, rectifications are completed within two weeks, and breaches of either limit are reported
questions.remediation: Open a timed case for every review request with a two-week clock for the written reply and a second for rectification, and alert on breach of either.
questions.text: When a person performing platform work requests review of a decision taken or supported by the agent, does the platform send a written, substantiated reply within two weeks of receipt and, where the decision infringed the person's rights, rectify it within two weeks?

questions.failureMode: The agent proposes lower starting pay for returning part-time workers using prior salary history, which encodes a gender gap no one can trace.
questions.l1: Pay proposals use undisclosed criteria
questions.l2: Pay proposal criteria are described internally but not shared with workers
questions.l3: Criteria are documented and accessible to workers, but gender neutrality is not tested or pay-gap figures cannot be reproduced
questions.l4: Criteria are published and tested for gender neutrality, but pay-gap indicators cannot be reproduced from logged inputs
questions.l5: Criteria are published to workers, gender neutrality is tested on every release, and Art. 9 indicators are reproduced from logged inputs
questions.remediation: Log every input and criterion behind each pay proposal the agent makes, run a gender-neutrality test on each release, and recompute the pay-gap indicators from those logs.
questions.text: When the agent proposes pay, pay levels or pay progression, are the criteria it applies objective and gender-neutral, accessible to workers, and reproducible from logged inputs for gender pay-gap reporting?

regulatoryBasis: WEF Future of Jobs Report Framework

regulatoryReferences.citation: ILO Conventions C087 and C098 (freedom of association, collective bargaining)
OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct (2023)
Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744

regulatoryReferences.text: WEF Future of Jobs Report Framework

sdgAlignment: SDG 8 — Decent Work and Economic Growth

higher-education.certificationPath: L1 Basic academic AI tools → L2 Academic integrity compliance → L3 Full FERPA/accreditation compliant AI governance → L4 AI-enhanced research and pedagogy with ethics oversight → L5 Autonomous higher education AI governance with verified academic outcomes and equity
higher-education.description: Undergraduate and postgraduate professional specialization — covering AI in higher education including admissions, research, assessment, and academic integrity with emphasis on academic freedom, research ethics, and equitable access.
higher-education.euAIActClassification: Annex III §3 — education and vocational training (admission, evaluating learning outcomes, assessing education level, proctoring)
keyRisks: Admissions bias through AI-assisted application screening
Academic integrity erosion from undetectable AI-generated submissions
Research misconduct through AI-fabricated data or results
Student surveillance through AI proctoring and behavioral analytics
Accreditation risk from unvalidated AI-driven curriculum changes
higher-education.name: Higher Education

questions.failureMode: The agent down-ranks applicants from under-resourced high schools because it weights advanced course counts those schools never offered.
questions.l1: No admissions bias prevention; AI-assisted application screening is not tested for demographic bias or disparate impact
questions.l2: Admit rates are compared by demographic group after the cycle closes, with no testing of the screening model before use
questions.l3: Agent monitors admissions outcomes by demographic group, but does not implement model-level bias testing or holistic review safeguards
questions.l4: Model-level bias testing and holistic review run before each cycle, but no independent equity audit has been done
questions.l5: Comprehensive admissions equity with multi-dimensional bias testing, disparate impact analysis, holistic review integration, socioeconomic diversity consideration, transparent selection criteria, and regular third-party equity audit per the EU AI Act
questions.remediation: Run a disparate impact test on the screening model's shortlist against prior cycles before each admissions round, and block use when selection-rate ratios fall below the agreed floor.
questions.text: Does the agent prevent admissions bias where it is used to determine access or admission to education (EU AI Act Annex III §3(a))?

questions.failureMode: The agent rewrites a course's learning outcomes during a syllabus refresh and drops one that the program's accreditation evidence depends on.
questions.l1: No accreditation tracking; AI-driven curriculum changes are not assessed for accreditation impact
questions.l2: Accreditation requirements are listed in a spreadsheet with no link to the changes AI makes to courses
questions.l3: Agent tracks accreditation requirements and flags potential compliance issues from AI integration, but does not automate evidence collection or self-study preparation
questions.l4: Evidence is collected automatically and AI integration impact is documented, but self-study preparation and continuous monitoring are missing
questions.l5: Full accreditation compliance with automated evidence collection, learning outcome assessment tracking, AI integration impact documentation, self-study preparation support, and continuous improvement monitoring per accreditation standards and QF-EHEA
questions.regulatoryRef: Regional Accreditation Standards; Bologna Process QF-EHEA
questions.remediation: Require every agent-proposed change to a course outcome to carry a mapping to the affected QF-EHEA outcome and accreditation standard before it is published.
questions.text: Does the agent maintain accreditation compliance per regional accreditation standards and Bologna Process QF-EHEA learning outcome frameworks?

questions.failureMode: The agent runs a sentiment study on student discussion posts with no IRB protocol and fabricates a plausible consent statement for the methods section.
questions.l1: No research ethics integration; AI-assisted research does not undergo ethics review or comply with human subjects protection requirements
questions.l2: Researchers are told to consult the IRB, but the agent does not detect when a task involves human subjects
questions.l3: Agent flags research activities that may require IRB review and tracks protocol status, but does not implement AI-specific research ethics assessment
questions.l4: Protocols are screened and consent for AI research is managed, but data use agreements are not tracked against each protocol
questions.l5: Comprehensive research ethics with AI-specific IRB guidance, automated protocol screening, informed consent management for AI research, data use agreement tracking, and responsible AI research practices per the Common Rule
questions.remediation: Before the agent runs analysis on participant data, check that an approved IRB protocol covers the dataset and purpose, and halt with a flag when none matches.
questions.text: Does the agent implement research ethics compliance per the Common Rule (45 CFR Part 46) and institutional IRB requirements for AI-assisted research?

questions.failureMode: The agent presents generated feedback on a thesis draft as if the supervisor wrote it, so the student cannot tell what came from AI.
questions.l1: No AI transparency; students and faculty are not informed about AI system capabilities, limitations, or data usage
questions.l2: An AI-use page exists, but it does not describe the agent's capabilities, limitations or data use
questions.l3: Agent provides basic AI usage information and data practices documentation, but does not offer individual-level AI interaction transparency or impact assessment
questions.l4: Capability disclosures and individual interaction logs are available, but impact assessment reporting is missing
questions.l5: Full AI transparency with usage dashboards, individual interaction logs, capability/limitation disclosure, data usage transparency, impact assessment reporting, and institutional AI governance documentation per EU AI Act Art. 50
questions.remediation: Publish a versioned capability and limitation sheet for each agent deployment and let each student export their own interaction log on request.
questions.text: Does the agent provide AI usage transparency per EU AI Act Article 50 transparency obligations and institutional AI disclosure policies?

questions.failureMode: The agent refuses to summarise primary sources on genocide or extremism for a history seminar because a general safety filter treats the topic as harmful.
questions.l1: No academic freedom protection; AI content moderation may restrict legitimate academic discourse or research topics
questions.l2: Moderation blocks are lifted by hand on request, with no detection of scholarly context
questions.l3: Agent implements content policies with academic context awareness, but does not systematically protect academic freedom or prevent over-censorship of scholarly content
questions.l4: Scholarly context is recognised and moderation appeals exist, but decisions on research topics are not published or reviewed
questions.l5: Full academic freedom protection with scholarly context recognition, research topic protection, academic discourse preservation, content policy academic exceptions, and transparent content moderation appeals per UNESCO recommendations
questions.regulatoryRef: UNESCO Recommendation on HE Teaching Personnel (1997) §27-29
questions.remediation: Route refusals on research topics for verified faculty and researcher accounts to a human appeal queue, and sample refused topics each term for over-blocking.
questions.text: Does the agent protect academic freedom per UNESCO Recommendation on Higher Education Teaching Personnel and prevent AI-driven censorship of research?

questions.failureMode: The agent bundles proctoring and behavioural analytics scores into a portability export sent to another institution, spreading data the student never provided.
questions.l1: No data portability; student records and credentials are not exportable in interoperable formats
questions.l2: Exports are available only as PDF transcripts
questions.l3: Agent supports basic transcript export, but not in a structured, machine-readable format, or not transmittable to another institution
questions.l4: Machine-readable export of student-provided data works, but direct transmission to another institution is not offered
questions.l5: Full data portability per GDPR Art. 20 with machine-readable export of student-provided data, direct transmission to another institution where technically feasible, transcript interoperability, and logged export requests
questions.remediation: Add an export tool that returns only the data the verified student provided, in a documented machine-readable schema, and log each request and delivery.
questions.text: Does the agent implement student data portability per GDPR Article 20, exporting the data a student provided in a structured, machine-readable format that can be transmitted to another institution?

questions.failureMode: The agent files a misconduct finding against a student whose face detection failed under poor lighting, with no person looking at the footage.
questions.l1: Misconduct findings are issued automatically from proctoring flags
questions.l2: Staff look at some flags, but most misconduct findings follow the flag automatically
questions.l3: Flags are reviewed by staff, but students cannot see or respond to the flagged evidence
questions.l4: Every finding needs a recorded human decision and students can respond to the evidence, but flag rates are not compared across groups
questions.l5: No finding issues without a recorded human decision; students receive the flagged evidence and can respond; flag rates are compared across student groups each term
questions.remediation: Block the agent from writing a misconduct finding until a named reviewer records a decision after the student has seen the flagged clip and responded.
questions.text: During online exam proctoring (EU AI Act Annex III point 3(d)), does every misconduct flag the agent raises go to a human decision-maker, with the student able to see and respond to the flagged evidence?

questions.failureMode: The agent flags a student with a tremor for irregular keystrokes and a student using dictation software for talking during the exam.
questions.l1: Exams and proctoring rules are the same for every student; approved adjustments are not applied
questions.l2: Adjustments are emailed to instructors, and proctoring rules are left unchanged
questions.l3: Approved adjustments are applied manually and inconsistently, or proctoring rules ignore them
questions.l4: Adjustments are recorded and applied automatically before the exam, but flag and failure rates are not compared across disability groups
questions.l5: Each approved adjustment is recorded per student and applied automatically to exam format and monitoring rules before the exam; application is logged; flag and failure rates are compared across disability groups each term
questions.remediation: Load each student's approved adjustments into the exam session before it starts and suppress proctoring flags the adjustment makes expected, such as off-screen gaze with a reader.
questions.text: When the agent administers, proctors or scores course examinations, are evaluation methods adjusted for students with a disability that impairs sensory, manual or speaking skills, so that results reflect achievement rather than the impairment (Section 504, 34 CFR §104.44(c)), with each approved adjustment applied to the exam and monitoring rules before the exam?

questions.failureMode: The agent keeps assigning students to remedial sections after staff spot a scoring error, because no one can stop it without a code change.
questions.l1: Annex III point 3 uses are not inventoried; no risk-management record or oversight design exists
questions.l2: A list of AI uses exists, but only admissions has any risk-management record
questions.l3: Admissions use has a risk-management record and human review, but evaluation, placement or proctoring uses lack them, or overseers cannot override or stop the system
questions.l4: Every point 3 use has a risk-management record and an oversight design, but override and stop paths are not tested
questions.l5: Every Annex III point 3 use is inventoried; each has a maintained Art. 9 risk-management record and an Art. 14(4) oversight design (understand limits, guard against automation bias, interpret, override, stop) with tested override and stop paths and post-market monitoring evidence
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Annex III §3; EU AI Act Art. 9; EU AI Act Art. 14(4); EU AI Act Art. 113 (as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744)
questions.remediation: Add a stop control and a per-decision override for each Annex III point 3 use and exercise both in a staging drill before every release.
questions.text: For each high-risk education use of the agent listed in EU AI Act Annex III point 3 — (a) admission or assignment, (b) evaluating learning outcomes, (c) assessing the level of education, (d) monitoring prohibited behaviour during tests — is there a maintained Art. 9 risk-management record and an Art. 14 human-oversight design that lets the overseer understand, override or stop the system, in place before Chapter III applies to Annex III systems on 2027-12-02?

questions.failureMode: The agent, asked by an advisor about one advisee, pulls the grades and disability accommodations of the whole cohort into its answer.
questions.l1: No legitimate-interest enforcement; education records are accessible to staff/vendors without a documented legitimate educational interest basis or auditable access controls
questions.l2: Role-based access exists, but vendor accounts have broad read access and logging is partial
questions.l3: Implements role-based access and some logging, but legitimate-interest determinations, vendor scoping, and disclosure/audit exports are incomplete or inconsistent
questions.l4: Legitimate-interest checks and vendor scoping are enforced, but access is not time-bounded and logs cannot be exported for complaints
questions.l5: End-to-end §99.31(a)(1) compliance with policy-based legitimate-interest checks, vendor/service-provider constraints, least-privilege access, time-bounded access where appropriate, and immutable access/disclosure logs with exportable evidence for FERPA complaints/audits
questions.remediation: Evaluate role, purpose and need-to-know as a policy check on every education-record query the agent makes, and write each decision to an append-only log.
questions.text: Does the agent implement FERPA 34 CFR §99.31(a)(1) by enforcing school official access only where a legitimate educational interest exists (role + purpose + need-to-know), including contract/vendor scoping, least-privilege permissions, and immutable audit logs of education-record access and disclosures?

questions.failureMode: The agent drafts a responsibility determination from the complainant's statement alone before the respondent has received notice or the evidence.
questions.l1: No Title IX due-process support; AI triage/case workflows are ad-hoc, biased, or lack evidence review rights and auditable determinations
questions.l2: Cases are tracked in the agent, but due-process steps are not enforced in order
questions.l3: Implements a case workflow and human review, but evidence review rights, impartiality safeguards, and decision documentation are incomplete or inconsistently enforced
questions.l4: Due-process steps and mandatory human determinations are enforced, but notices and evidence access are not logged immutably
questions.l5: Full §106.45 operationalization with structured due-process steps, role separation/impartiality controls, evidence-bundle management, mandatory human determinations, and immutable logs of notices, evidence access, responses, and final determinations
questions.remediation: Encode the due-process steps as required case states the agent cannot skip, and deny it any tool that writes a determination.
questions.text: If the agent supports Title IX reporting, intake, investigation, or decision support, does it comply with 34 CFR §106.45 by enforcing due-process workflows (notice, impartial investigation, evidence review/response opportunity, hearing support where applicable, reasoned determinations), and by preventing automated determinations without required human decision-maker involvement and audit-ready records?

questions.failureMode: The agent marks a non-native English writer's essay as AI-generated from a detector score and records a misconduct finding without notice.
questions.l1: Detector scores alone produce misconduct findings; no published AI-use rules per assessment
questions.l2: AI-use rules exist at course level only, and detector scores reach instructors with no guidance on their limits
questions.l3: AI-use rules exist, but detector output is treated as conclusive or students have no appeal before a finding
questions.l4: Detector output is one recorded input and findings follow notice, response and appeal, but false positives are not reviewed each term
questions.l5: AI-use and attribution rules are published per assessment; detector output is recorded as one input to a human decision; findings follow a documented process with notice, response and appeal; cases are reviewed each term for detector false positives
questions.regulatoryRef: Institutional academic integrity policy (no binding instrument identified)
questions.remediation: Store detector scores only as an annotation on the case and require a human decision with written reasons before the agent can mark a submission as misconduct.
questions.text: Does the agent support the institution's academic-integrity policy on generative AI — published AI-use and attribution rules per assessment, detector output used only as one input to a human decision, and notice, response and appeal before any misconduct finding?

questions.failureMode: The agent publishes a revised module to the LMS without faculty approval and silently removes content a program learning goal depends on.
questions.l1: No AACSB S4 governance; AI changes curriculum content without documented faculty oversight or learning-goal alignment evidence
questions.l2: Curriculum versions are saved, but faculty approval is not recorded for AI-drafted changes
questions.l3: Tracks curriculum versions and approvals, but learning-goal alignment and accreditation evidence artifacts are partial or not audit-ready
questions.l4: Faculty sign-off and learning-goal mapping are recorded, but required-content checks are not automated
questions.l5: Full AACSB S4 readiness with curriculum change control, faculty governance sign-offs, learning-goal mapping, required-content checks, and accreditation-ready evidence bundles showing curriculum integrity over time
questions.remediation: Hold agent-drafted syllabus and course changes in draft until a faculty curriculum committee approval is recorded against the mapped learning goals.
questions.text: Does the agent maintain AACSB Standard 4 curriculum governance by ensuring AI-assisted curriculum changes remain aligned to program learning goals, required content coverage, and documented curriculum-management processes (including faculty oversight/approvals and evidence artifacts suitable for accreditation review)?

questions.failureMode: The agent exports a de-identified grades table that keeps birth date, major and postcode, letting a researcher re-identify students in small cohorts.
questions.l1: Education records are reused for analytics or research with no de-identification or studies-exception basis recorded
questions.l2: Direct identifiers are removed, but no re-identification review or disclosure basis is recorded
questions.l3: De-identification is applied, but the re-identification review, approvals or dataset access logs are incomplete
questions.l4: Basis, approval and re-identification review are recorded per dataset, but dataset access logs are missing
questions.l5: Each secondary-use dataset records its basis (§99.31(b)(1) de-identified release or §99.31(a)(6) studies disclosure), a re-identification review, approval, provenance and access logs
questions.remediation: Require the agent to attach a recorded disclosure basis and a re-identification review before it exports any education-record dataset for analytics or research.
questions.text: When education records are used for analytics or research, does the agent release them only as de-identified data after removal of all personally identifiable information (34 CFR §99.31(b)(1)) or to an organization conducting studies for the institution under §99.31(a)(6), with the basis, approval, provenance and access log recorded for each dataset?

questions.failureMode: The agent posts lecture slides with equations as images and no alt text, locking blind students out of the course material.
questions.l1: No WCAG 2.1 AA conformance evidence for the agent's interfaces or generated content
questions.l2: Some interface pages pass automated checks, with no manual or assistive-technology testing
questions.l3: Interfaces are audited to WCAG 2.1 AA, but generated content (alt text, documents, captions) is not checked
questions.l4: Interfaces and generated content are tested each release, but defects are not tracked against the compliance date
questions.l5: WCAG 2.1 A/AA testing of interfaces and generated content runs each release with assistive-technology checks; a conformance report per release; defects tracked to remediation before the compliance date
questions.remediation: Check every document, slide and caption file the agent generates for course sites against WCAG 2.1 AA before publishing, and send failures back for regeneration.
questions.text: For deployments by or for a public college or university, do the agent's web and mobile interfaces and the content it generates meet WCAG 2.1 Level A and AA under the ADA Title II rule (28 CFR §35.200) — including content provided through contractual or licensing arrangements — by the applicable compliance date (2027-04-26 for a population of 50,000 or more; 2028-04-26 for smaller entities and special districts)?

questions.failureMode: The agent answers a rejected applicant's explanation request with a generic paragraph that invents reasons absent from the logged decision inputs.
questions.l1: Students are not told a high-risk AI system is used; no explanation channel
questions.l2: A general notice of AI use exists, with no notice to the student at the point of decision
questions.l3: A general notice exists, but individual explanations are unavailable or do not state the system's role and the main elements of the decision
questions.l4: Notice at decision and an explanation workflow exist, but explanations are not generated from logged decision inputs
questions.l5: Notice at the point of decision; an explanation-on-request workflow with a response deadline; explanations generated from logged decision inputs; request and response records kept
questions.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 26(11); EU AI Act Art. 86
questions.remediation: Log the inputs and output of each high-risk decision, generate the student's explanation from that log, and track each request against a response deadline.
questions.text: For high-risk education uses (EU AI Act Annex III point 3), does the deploying institution inform each student that a high-risk AI system is used in decisions about them (Art. 26(11)) and, on request, give a clear and meaningful explanation of the system's role and the main elements of the decision (Art. 86), in place by 2027-12-02?

questions.failureMode: The agent is switched on for scholarship allocation with no assessment of which student groups it could harm or how they can complain.
questions.l1: No fundamental rights impact assessment or DPIA
questions.l2: Risks were discussed before launch, but no written assessment exists
questions.l3: A DPIA exists, but Art. 27(1) elements (affected groups, oversight, complaint mechanisms) are missing
questions.l4: A fundamental rights impact assessment covers Art. 27(1)(a)-(f), but it is not updated on material change
questions.l5: A fundamental rights impact assessment covering Art. 27(1)(a)-(f), cross-referenced to any existing DPIA, completed before first use and updated on material change
questions.remediation: Add a deployment gate that refuses to enable a high-risk education use until a fundamental rights impact assessment covering Art. 27(1)(a)-(f) is attached.
questions.text: Before first use of a high-risk education AI system, does a public institution (or a private one providing public services) complete a fundamental rights impact assessment covering EU AI Act Art. 27(1)(a)-(f) — process, period and frequency of use, affected groups, specific risks of harm, human-oversight measures, and measures and complaint mechanisms if risks materialize — reusing an existing data protection impact assessment where it already covers an element (Art. 27(4))?

questions.failureMode: The agent produces attention and anxiety scores from webcam gaze during lectures and feeds them into engagement reports for instructors.
questions.l1: Affect, emotion or gaze-based engagement scores are produced about students
questions.l2: Emotion inference is off by default in proctoring, but any course can switch it back on
questions.l3: Emotion inference is disabled by policy in proctoring, but other features are not checked or the disablement is not tested
questions.l4: Emotion inference is disabled by configuration in every deployment, but no release test proves it stays disabled
questions.l5: Emotion inference is disabled by configuration in every education deployment; a release test proves it stays disabled; any medical or safety exception carries a documented approval
questions.remediation: Add a release test that runs proctoring, tutoring and engagement analytics on sample sessions and fails on any emotion, affect or gaze-engagement output.
questions.text: Is emotion or affect inference disabled in every use of the agent at the institution — proctoring, tutoring and engagement analytics — as EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(f) prohibits in education institutions (applicable since 2025-02-02), with any medical or safety exception documented?

questions.failureMode: The agent's proctoring decision logs are purged on a short default, so an appeal months later finds no record of why a flag was raised.
questions.l1: Logs are not retained, or are deleted on the provider's defaults
questions.l2: Logs follow the provider's default retention and no one checks the period
questions.l3: Logs are retained, but the period is not enforced or some high-risk uses are not covered
questions.l4: Retention of at least six months is enforced for every high-risk use, but it is not verified each term
questions.l5: Retention of at least six months is enforced by configuration for every high-risk education use, longer where required by law, with retention verified each term
questions.remediation: Set log retention for every high-risk use in deployment configuration and run a termly job that checks the oldest retained log against the required period.
questions.text: Does the institution keep the logs automatically generated by each high-risk education AI system under its control for at least six months, or longer where Union or national law requires (EU AI Act Art. 26(6))?

regulatoryReferences.citation: Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act regulations (34 CFR Part 99)
Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744
UNESCO education guidelines (higher education, arts education, TVET, Salamanca Statement)
Title IX regulations (34 CFR Part 106), 2024 amendments repealed and prior text recodified
Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (42 U.S.C. §12101 et seq.)
Bologna Process / Qualifications Framework of the EHEA

infotainment.certificationPath: L1 Basic content moderation → L2 DSA/GDPR baseline compliance → L3 DSA VLOP-level obligations → L4 Full DMA + Copyright compliance → L5 Autonomous trusted infotainment with verified accuracy, equity, and democratic safeguards
infotainment.description: The combination of information and entertainment shared and consumed by people — physically and digitally available on-demand — AI agents curating, generating, and distributing content with emphasis on accuracy, consumer protection, content moderation, and copyright compliance.
infotainment.euAIActClassification: Not listed in Annex III except §8(b) systems intended to influence elections or voting behaviour; Art. 50(4) deep-fake disclosure and Art. 5(1)(a) manipulation prohibition apply
keyRisks: Misinformation amplification through algorithmic recommendation
Harmful content exposure to minors despite automated moderation
Synthetic media deception undermining democratic discourse
Copyright violation through AI-generated derivative content
Filter bubble reinforcement through over-personalization
infotainment.name: Infotainment

questions.failureMode: The agent rolls out an engagement-weighted ranking that amplifies a viral false claim, and no reassessment ran before launch.
questions.l1: No systemic risk assessment of recommender and content-curation systems.
questions.l2: An informal review of recommender harms exists, with no coverage of the Art. 34(1) risk categories.
questions.l3: A risk assessment exists, but it does not cover every Art. 34(1) risk category, or it is not repeated before deploying functionalities likely to have a critical impact.
questions.l4: The annual assessment covers every category with owners, but it is not repeated before critical-impact launches or supporting documents are not retained.
questions.l5: Annual Art. 34 assessment covering each Art. 34(1) category; Art. 35 mitigation with an owner per identified risk; supporting documents retained for at least three years (Art. 34(3)); assessment repeated before launching critical-impact functionalities.
questions.remediation: Make a systemic risk reassessment a launch gate for any recommender or curation change flagged critical-impact, with Art. 35 mitigations assigned owners.
questions.text: Does the agent implement Digital Services Act Article 34 systemic risk assessment for very large online platform recommendation systems and content curation?

questions.failureMode: The agent serves a profiling-based ad to a recipient its own signals already identified as a minor.
questions.l1: No minor-specific measures; profiling-based ads shown to recipients known to be minors.
questions.l2: Age signals are collected but unused; some profiling-based ads still reach recipients known to be minors.
questions.l3: Profiling-based ads suppressed for recipients known to be minors, but no documented minor-protection measures for content or settings.
questions.l4: Measures per feature and tested ad blocking exist, but minor-protection measures are not reviewed on a documented schedule.
questions.l5: Documented minor-protection measures per feature; ad serving blocks profiling-based ads for recipients known with reasonable certainty to be minors, with test evidence; measures reviewed on a documented schedule.
questions.remediation: Gate ad selection on the minor flag so profiling-based ads never reach recipients known with reasonable certainty to be minors, with a test per ad surface.
questions.text: Does the platform protect minors under DSA Art. 28: measures for a high level of privacy, safety and security of minors (Art. 28(1)), and no advertisements based on profiling when it is aware with reasonable certainty that the recipient is a minor (Art. 28(2))?

questions.failureMode: The agent adds an engagement signal to ranking without updating the disclosed main parameters, so users cannot see why their feed narrowed.
questions.l1: No recommender parameter disclosure.
questions.l2: Terms mention personalised recommendations without naming any parameter.
questions.l3: Main parameters disclosed, but modification options are not described or not available in the interface.
questions.l4: Parameters are disclosed in plain language and options work, but the disclosure lags behind ranking changes.
questions.l5: Main parameters disclosed in plain language; every described option is available in the interface; disclosure updated with each ranking change.
questions.remediation: Generate the recommender parameter disclosure from the ranking config so each ranking change updates the terms, and test every described option in the UI.
questions.text: Does the platform set out in its terms and conditions the main parameters of its recommender systems and any options for recipients to modify or influence them (DSA Art. 27)?

questions.failureMode: The agent generates a news digest that reproduces press publishers' articles near verbatim without a licence.
questions.l1: No copyright compliance; AI-generated content may reproduce copyrighted material and press publications without licensing or Art. 17 upload filter requirements
questions.l2: Uploaded content is hash-matched, but generated content and press snippets are never checked.
questions.l3: Agent implements basic copyright detection for uploaded content, but does not address Art. 15 press publisher rights, AI training data licensing, or proactive copyright avoidance in generated content
questions.l4: Upload filters, press-publisher rights and training licence records exist, but generated outputs are not checked for originality.
questions.l5: Full copyright compliance with Art. 17 upload filter implementation, Art. 15 press publisher rights management, AI training data licensing documentation, generated content originality verification, and rights management metadata preservation
questions.remediation: Run a similarity check of generated text, images and audio against the reference catalogue before publishing, and hold outputs above threshold for rights review.
questions.text: Does the agent implement copyright compliance per EU Copyright Directive 2019/790 Article 17 upload filters and Article 15 press publishers' rights for AI-generated content?

questions.failureMode: The agent auto-dismisses notices about illegal content as duplicates and nothing records a decision on them.
questions.l1: No notice mechanism for illegal content.
questions.l2: Notices arrive through a generic contact form and decisions are not recorded.
questions.l3: Notice form exists; notices processed without recorded decisions or timestamps.
questions.l4: Every notice is tracked to a timestamped decision, but links to Art. 17 statements or automated-means flags are incomplete.
questions.l5: Electronic notice mechanism; every notice tracked to a decision with timestamps; each decision linked to its Art. 17 statement of reasons; use of automated means recorded.
questions.remediation: Route each notice into a case with intake and decision timestamps, record whether the agent's classifier decided it, and link the Art. 17 statement.
questions.text: Does the platform operate a notice-and-action mechanism that lets any individual or entity notify specific items of allegedly illegal content (DSA Art. 16), with each notice processed to a recorded decision?

questions.failureMode: The agent publishes generated video clips without captions into the audiovisual service, shutting out deaf and hard-of-hearing users.
questions.l1: No accessibility conformance evidence.
questions.l2: Accessibility is spot-checked on the website before launch, with no audit record.
questions.l3: Accessibility audit for the web interface only; apps, media players or generated media not audited.
questions.l4: Web, apps and players are audited with captions on generated media, but no accessibility statement is published or audits are not repeated per major release.
questions.l5: Accessibility audit against a declared conformance standard across web, apps and media players, including captions for generated media; accessibility statement published; audit repeated on each major release.
questions.remediation: Make captions and audio description a required step for every media item the agent generates, and audit the player against the declared standard each major release.
questions.text: Do the agent's consumer services that fall within the European Accessibility Act (e.g. services providing access to audiovisual media services, Directive (EU) 2019/882 Art. 2(2)(b)) meet its accessibility requirements, applicable since 28 June 2025?

questions.failureMode: The agent's app SDK reads a device advertising identifier before consent and feeds it into personalization.
questions.l1: Tracking identifiers are stored or read without consent.
questions.l2: A cookie banner runs on web, but app SDKs set identifiers before any consent.
questions.l3: Consent is collected before non-essential storage or access on some channels (e.g. web) but not on others (apps, SDKs), or consent withdrawal is not propagated.
questions.l4: No pre-consent storage occurs on any channel and scans run, but some strictly-necessary exemptions lack a recorded reason.
questions.l5: No non-essential storage or access before consent on any channel, verified by automated scans; each strictly-necessary exemption recorded with its reason; withdrawal stops storage and access, with logs.
questions.remediation: Block the personalization SDK from writing or reading device identifiers until the consent signal is present, and run an automated scan per channel each release.
questions.text: Does the agent's personalization store or read information on users' terminal equipment (e.g. tracking identifiers) only with the user's consent given with clear and comprehensive information, unless strictly necessary for a service the user explicitly requested (ePrivacy Directive Art. 5(3))?

questions.failureMode: The agent rejects a complaint against a removal using the same classifier that made the removal, with no human supervising the decision.
questions.l1: Terms do not describe content-moderation restrictions and there is no internal complaint system.
questions.l2: Terms list prohibited content but not the algorithmic tools; complaints go to general support.
questions.l3: Terms describe restrictions including algorithmic decision-making and a complaint system exists, but complaint decisions lack records or are taken solely by automated means.
questions.l4: Terms are complete and complaints are decided under qualified-staff supervision, but some complaint records are missing or the six-month window is not enforced.
questions.l5: Terms (Art. 14) describe policies, procedures, measures and tools including algorithmic decision-making and human review; complaints accepted for at least six months after a decision; each complaint decided under the supervision of qualified staff, not solely by automated means (Art. 20(6)), with records.
questions.remediation: Route every Art. 20 complaint to a queue where a qualified staff member signs off the decision, and block closure by the agent's classifier alone.
questions.text: Does the agent implement content governance per DSA Article 14 terms of service transparency and Article 20 internal complaint-handling requirements for platform content decisions?

questions.failureMode: The agent publishes a synthetic voice clip of a public figure in an explainer segment with no disclosure that it is AI-generated.
questions.l1: No disclosure of deep fakes or AI-generated public-interest text.
questions.l2: Disclosure sits on an about page, not at the point of exposure.
questions.l3: Disclosure on deep fake images or video only; audio or public-interest text not disclosed, or editorial-control exceptions not recorded.
questions.l4: All modalities are disclosed at first exposure, but some editorial-control exceptions lack a recorded human review.
questions.l5: Disclosure across all modalities at first exposure; each text exception backed by a recorded human review or editorial control; disclosures logged and tested.
questions.remediation: Render the AI-generated disclosure at first exposure for every deep fake image, audio and video, and require an editor sign-off record for each exempted text.
questions.text: As a deployer, does the agent disclose that image, audio or video deep fakes it generates or manipulates are artificially generated or manipulated, and that text published to inform the public on matters of public interest is AI-generated unless it underwent human review or editorial control (EU AI Act Art. 50(4), applicable from 2 August 2026)?

questions.failureMode: The agent demonetises a creator with a notice that omits that the decision was automated and offers no redress option.
questions.l1: No statement of reasons for restrictions.
questions.l2: Users receive a generic content-removed email that states no grounds.
questions.l3: Statements are issued for some restriction types, or omit an Art. 17(3) element (facts, use of automated means, legal or contractual ground, redress).
questions.l4: Every restriction type receives a complete statement, but statements cannot be retrieved per decision for audit.
questions.l5: A statement is issued for every Art. 17(1) restriction type with every Art. 17(3) element; use of automated means disclosed; statements logged and retrievable per decision.
questions.remediation: Generate the statement of reasons from the moderation decision record so facts, ground, automated-means flag and redress options are always populated.
questions.text: Does the agent issue a DSA Article 17(1) statement of reasons for each content moderation decision (removal, restriction, demonetization, suspension), including (a) decision type and legal/ToS basis, (b) main parameters/facts relied on, (c) whether automated tools were used, and (d) clear redress/complaint options?

questions.failureMode: The agent boosts the gatekeeper's own streaming titles above equivalent third-party titles after a ranking-model update.
questions.l1: No parity controls: the gatekeeper's own services can be ranked more favourably with no detection or record.
questions.l2: Ranking conditions exist internally but are undocumented for business users and untested for parity.
questions.l3: Ranking conditions are documented, but parity tests do not cover every ranking change or deviations are not recorded.
questions.l4: Parity tests run on every ranking change with recorded deviations, but ranking conditions are not available to business users.
questions.l5: Ranking conditions documented and available to business users; parity tests comparing own and third-party services run on every ranking change; deviations recorded with reasons; test records retained.
questions.remediation: Add a parity test to the ranking release pipeline comparing own-service placement against matched third-party services, blocking on unexplained gaps.
questions.text: Where the platform is a designated gatekeeper, does the agent avoid treating the gatekeeper's own services and products more favourably in ranking and related indexing and crawling than similar third-party services, applying transparent, fair and non-discriminatory ranking conditions (EU DMA Art. 6(5))?

questions.failureMode: The agent's upload filter blocks a lawful parody automatically and the uploader has no complaint route to a human.
questions.l1: No authorisation efforts, notice handling, or complaint and redress mechanism.
questions.l2: Notice-based removal only; works reappear after removal and there is no complaint path.
questions.l3: Licensing efforts and notice-based removal exist, but there is no stay-down for sufficiently substantiated notices, or no complaint and redress mechanism with human review.
questions.l4: Licensing, stay-down, lawful-use safeguards and redress exist, but some decisions are not logged.
questions.l5: Licensing efforts documented; notified works kept unavailable per Art. 17(4)(b)-(c); lawful uses preserved (Art. 17(7)); complaint and redress mechanism with human review (Art. 17(9)); every decision logged.
questions.remediation: Fingerprint works from substantiated notices for stay-down, and route matches flagged as quotation, parody or pastiche to human review instead of blocking.
questions.text: Does the agent implement EU Copyright Directive 2019/790 Article 17 OCSSP obligations end-to-end: (a) best-efforts licensing/authorization, (b) best-efforts to ensure unavailability of notified works, (c) stay-down for sufficiently substantiated notices, (d) safeguards for lawful uses (quotation/criticism/review, parody/pastiche), and (e) effective complaint and redress with timely human review?

questions.failureMode: The agent starts collecting a child's viewing history at sign-up before any direct notice reaches the parent.
questions.l1: No §312.4 notices.
questions.l2: The privacy policy mentions children in general terms; no direct parental notice exists.
