questions.text: Does the agent enforce RoHS Directive 2011/65/EU Article 4 by gating release/placing-on-the-market decisions on product-level RoHS compliance evidence (including BOM aggregation, supplier declarations, test evidence, and exemption applicability tracking)?

questions.failureMode: The agent publishes treatment information from an older design that omits a newly added battery, so a recycler shreds it and starts a fire.
questions.l1: No treatment information is published for new equipment types
questions.l2: Treatment information exists for a few product lines, written by hand from drawings
questions.l3: Treatment information exists for some product lines but is not linked to product types or launch dates
questions.l4: Per-type records are generated from the BOM and published within a year, but design changes do not create a new version
questions.l5: Per-type treatment records generated from the bill of materials, published to treatment facilities within one year of market placement, versioned on design changes and cross-checked with the Digital Product Passport
questions.remediation: Generate treatment information per equipment type from the BOM, including dangerous-substance locations, and republish it on every design change.
questions.text: Does the agent provide treatment facilities with the reuse and treatment information required by WEEE Directive 2012/19/EU Article 15 (components, materials and the location of dangerous substances) for each new type of electrical and electronic equipment within one year of placing it on the market?

questions.failureMode: The agent auto-patches an actively exploited firmware flaw across connected appliances and closes the ticket, so the CRA report is never started.
questions.l1: No path to report vulnerabilities or incidents in agent-managed products
questions.l2: Vulnerabilities are tracked internally, but no one owns reporting to the Single Reporting Platform
questions.l3: A manual reporting path to the Single Reporting Platform exists, but timing has not been tested
questions.l4: Reporting to the platform is rehearsed and timed, but final-report content is still assembled by hand
questions.l5: Detection-to-report is rehearsed and timed against 24h/72h, final-report content (corrective measure, root cause) is assembled from agent and product logs, and each report is retained
questions.regulatoryRef: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 (manufacturer reporting of actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents)
questions.remediation: Open a reporting case with 24h and 72h timers when an exploited vulnerability is confirmed in a managed product, and draft final-report content from logs.
questions.text: Can the manufacturer report an actively exploited vulnerability or severe incident affecting a connected product the agent runs on or manages through the CRA Single Reporting Platform within the Cyber Resilience Act deadlines (24h early warning, 72h notification, final report) applying from 11 Sep 2026?

regulatoryReferences.citation: European Commission, Circular Economy Action Plan, COM(2020) 98

networked-ecosystems.certificationPath: L1 Basic API security → L2 GDPR data portability compliance → L3 EU Data Act/DGA compliance → L4 Full ecosystem trust architecture → L5 Autonomous ecosystem orchestration with verified data rights and sovereignty
networked-ecosystems.description: Data connectivity across customer, enterprise, and industry ecosystems — flipping financial ecosystems to human ecosystems — AI agents orchestrating data flows, API ecosystems, and platform integrations with emphasis on interoperability, data rights, and ecosystem trust.
networked-ecosystems.euAIActClassification: Annex III §2 where a safety component of critical digital infrastructure; otherwise not listed — Art. 50 transparency applies
keyRisks: Data sovereignty erosion through ecosystem lock-in
API abuse enabling unauthorized data aggregation
Ecosystem monopolization through AI-managed data access
Privacy violations through ecosystem data correlation
Critical infrastructure dependency on single ecosystem providers
networked-ecosystems.name: Connectivity to Networked Ecosystems

questions.failureMode: The agent refuses a user's product data request by labelling the whole dataset a trade secret, without identifying it or agreeing protective measures.
questions.l1: Users cannot obtain product or related-service data.
questions.l2: Users can raise a support ticket for product data, but there is no defined request path or response record.
questions.l3: Data provided on manual request; no access by design for in-scope products placed on the market after 12 September 2026, or trade-secret withholding without documented agreed measures.
questions.l4: Access by design and a logged request path exist, but some trade-secret withholding lacks a documented identification or agreed measures.
questions.l5: Access by design (self-service interface with metadata) for in-scope products; request path with logged response times; every trade-secret withholding has a documented identification and agreed measures; access logs retained.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU Data Act Art. 3(1); EU Data Act Art. 4; EU Data Act Art. 4(6)
questions.remediation: Ship a self-service export for product and related-service data with metadata, and require a trade-secret identification record before the agent withholds a field.
questions.text: For connected products or related services, does the agent make product and related-service data accessible to the user by default (EU Data Act Art. 3(1), for products placed on the market after 12 September 2026) or on request (Art. 4), disclosing trade secrets only under agreed protective measures (Art. 4(6))?

questions.failureMode: The agent exposes a debug endpoint with verbose errors and permissive CORS during an integration rollout, and an outside caller harvests partner records.
questions.l1: No API inventory and no authorisation tests; object-level authorisation is not enforced.
questions.l2: Some endpoints check the caller's token but not object ownership; there is no API inventory.
questions.l3: Object-level authorisation (API1:2023) is enforced and tested on some endpoints; the other API Top 10 2023 categories are not mapped to tests.
questions.l4: Each API Top 10 category maps to a CI test and API8 checks run per deployment, but findings are not tracked to closure or agent-created endpoints are missing.
questions.l5: Every endpoint is inventoried (API9); each API Top 10 2023 category is mapped to an automated test in CI, including per-object authorisation tests; misconfiguration (API8) checks run on each deployment; findings tracked to closure.
questions.remediation: Generate the API inventory from the gateway, map each OWASP API Top 10 2023 category to a CI test, and run a misconfiguration scan on every deployment.
questions.text: Does the agent implement API security per OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 including broken object level authorization (API1) and security misconfiguration (API8) prevention?

questions.failureMode: The agent pulls intermediated partner data into the operator's own analytics features, reusing it for a purpose outside the intermediation service.
questions.l1: Intermediation service operated without notification; intermediated data reused for other purposes.
questions.l2: Intermediation is offered while the notification is still being prepared; reuse of intermediated data is not restricted.
questions.l3: Notification filed; separation or non-reuse controls exist on paper but are not technically enforced or evidenced.
questions.l4: Notification, separate legal person and technical reuse blocks are in place, but the Art. 12 condition-to-control map is not reviewed on a schedule.
questions.l5: Notification on file; separate legal person; technical controls block reuse of intermediated data with access logs; Art. 12 conditions mapped to controls and reviewed on a documented schedule.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU Data Governance Act Art. 11; EU Data Governance Act Art. 12
questions.remediation: Tag intermediated data at ingestion and enforce a policy that denies any agent query outside the intermediation service purpose, logging each denial.
questions.text: If the agent provides data intermediation services, has the provider notified the competent authority (EU Data Governance Act Art. 11), and does the agent meet the Art. 12 conditions, including not using the intermediated data for other purposes and providing the service through a separate legal person (Art. 12(a))?

questions.failureMode: The agent answers a portability request with a PDF summary, leaving the user unable to move their data to a competing service.
questions.l1: No machine-readable export of personal data.
questions.l2: Exports are PDF summaries or screenshots; nothing machine-readable is offered.
questions.l3: Machine-readable export for some data categories; no direct controller-to-controller transmission.
questions.l4: Machine-readable export covers all provided data with request logs, but direct controller-to-controller transmission is missing where feasible.
questions.l5: Export covers all personal data provided by the data subject where Art. 20(1) applies; direct transmission where technically feasible; each request logged with completion time.
questions.remediation: Produce Art. 20 exports in a documented JSON schema covering every provided-data category and add a direct transmit option to a receiving controller's endpoint.
questions.text: Does the agent let data subjects receive the personal data they provided in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format and transmit it to another controller without hindrance (GDPR Art. 20(1))?

questions.failureMode: The agent changes a response field in a partner API without updating the published description, breaking every third-party integration that relied on it.
questions.l1: Ecosystem APIs have no published interface description and data formats are undocumented.
questions.l2: Interface descriptions live in internal wikis only and drift from the running services.
questions.l3: Interface descriptions are published for some APIs, or data formats are documented but not openly available to ecosystem participants.
questions.l4: Every API has a published description and open formats, but CI does not validate descriptions against the running service or deprecations lack notice.
questions.l5: Every exposed API has a published machine-readable description validated in CI against the running service; every exchanged data format is openly documented and versioned; deprecations announced with a documented notice period.
questions.remediation: Publish an OpenAPI 3.1 description for every ecosystem API and add a CI contract test that fails when the running service diverges from it.
questions.text: Does the agent expose every ecosystem API with a published machine-readable interface description (for example OpenAPI 3.1) and exchange data in openly documented formats, applying the technical interoperability layer of the European Interoperability Framework (COM(2017) 134)?

questions.failureMode: The agent authenticates to partner APIs with a long-lived shared secret at the lowest assurance level and performs bulk exports no human identity could.
questions.l1: No assurance-level mapping.
questions.l2: Human logins use MFA, but no assurance level is documented for any identity class.
questions.l3: AAL mapped and enforced for human users; agent or workload identities, or federation (FAL), not mapped.
questions.l4: IAL, AAL and FAL are mapped and enforced with step-up, but the mapping is not re-reviewed when a new agent or federation partner is added.
questions.l5: IAL, AAL and FAL mapped for every human and agent identity class; enforcement tested; step-up authentication for sensitive operations; mapping reviewed on change.
questions.remediation: Assign each agent and workload identity class an AAL and FAL, issue short-lived credentials to match, and require step-up before sensitive ecosystem operations.
questions.text: Does the agent's ecosystem access management map human and agent identities to NIST SP 800-63-4 identity assurance (IAL), authenticator assurance (AAL) and federation assurance (FAL) levels and enforce them?

questions.failureMode: The agent forces a user who offers an EUDI Wallet through a proprietary identity check that collects more identity data than the flow needs.
questions.l1: No EUDI Wallet support on flows that require strong authentication.
questions.l2: Wallet acceptance is on the roadmap; strong-authentication flows accept proprietary methods only.
questions.l3: Wallet acceptance piloted on some flows; relying-party registration not completed.
questions.l4: Wallets are accepted on every strong-authentication flow with registration on file, but acceptance is not tested against the validation mechanisms.
questions.l5: Wallet authentication accepted on every flow requiring strong authentication; relying-party registration on file; acceptance tested against the wallet validation mechanisms.
questions.remediation: Add EUDI Wallet presentation as an option on each strong-authentication flow and test it against the wallet validation mechanisms before release.
questions.text: Where the operator is a private relying party, other than a micro or small enterprise, that Union or national law or a contract requires to use strong user authentication for online identification, does the agent accept European Digital Identity Wallets on the user's voluntary request (eIDAS 2.0, Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2024/1183, Art. 5f(2), no later than 36 months after the implementing acts under Arts. 5a(23) and 5c(6) enter into force), with the relying party registered under Art. 5b?

questions.failureMode: The agent grants faster API quotas and better placement to an affiliated partner while recording nothing a rival business user could contest.
questions.l1: No algorithmic transparency; ecosystem ranking, access, and data monetization decisions are opaque without fairness assessment
questions.l2: Ranking and access decisions are explained only on request, with no fairness assessment.
questions.l3: Agent provides basic transparency reports for ecosystem ranking and access decisions, but does not implement full DMA Art. 6(12) requirements or contestability mechanisms
questions.l4: Transparency reports, non-discrimination monitoring and contest routes exist, but business-user access audits or Art. 33 pricing transparency are missing.
questions.l5: Full DMA compliance with algorithmic transparency for ranking and access decisions, non-discrimination monitoring, business user access audits, contestability mechanisms, and transparent data access pricing per EU Data Act Art. 33
questions.regulatoryRef: EU DMA Art. 6(12); EU Data Act Art. 33
questions.remediation: Log every ranking and access decision the agent makes for business users with its parameters, and run a monthly disparity check across comparable business users.
questions.text: Does the agent implement algorithmic transparency per EU Digital Markets Act Article 6(12) for core platform services and fair access principles?

questions.failureMode: The agent quotes a competitor a higher data-access fee than a comparable recipient, with no documented basis for the difference.
questions.l1: Data made available on undocumented or discriminatory terms.
questions.l2: Terms are negotiated per recipient by email; there are no standard terms and no compensation basis.
questions.l3: Written terms exist, but the compensation basis is not documented, or differs between comparable recipients without a recorded reason.
questions.l4: Standard terms and a documented compensation calculation exist per category, but deviations are not always recorded with reasons.
questions.l5: Standard terms per recipient category; compensation calculation documented and applied consistently; deviations recorded with reasons; terms disclosed to the recipient before agreement.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU Data Act Art. 8(1); EU Data Act Art. 9(1)
questions.remediation: Have the agent quote B2B data terms only from the standard template for the recipient category and require a recorded reason for any compensation deviation.
questions.text: Where the agent makes data available to a data recipient in business-to-business relations under a Data Act obligation, does it agree fair, reasonable, non-discriminatory and transparent terms (EU Data Act Art. 8(1)) and set any compensation that is non-discriminatory and reasonable (Art. 9(1))?

questions.failureMode: The agent's public OAuth client obtains tokens through the implicit grant, and an intercepted redirect lets an attacker replay them against partner APIs.
questions.l1: Implicit grant in use, or public clients without PKCE.
questions.l2: PKCE is used by the newest clients, but a legacy single-page app still uses the implicit grant.
questions.l3: PKCE enforced for public clients and implicit grant removed, but at least one other applicable RFC 9700 requirement is not mapped to a test.
questions.l4: Every applicable RFC 9700 requirement has a conformance test, but authorization logs do not show PKCE on every request.
questions.l5: Every applicable RFC 9700 requirement for the client types in use is mapped to an automated conformance test in CI; logs show PKCE on every authorization.
questions.remediation: Reject public-client authorization requests that lack a PKCE code_challenge at the server, disable the implicit grant, and add RFC 9700 conformance tests in CI.
questions.text: Does the agent's OAuth integration conform to IETF RFC 9700 (BCP 240), including PKCE for every public client, which RFC 9700 makes a MUST, and no use of the implicit grant, which it says SHOULD NOT be used?

questions.failureMode: The agent joins intermediated data from two partners in a shared warehouse and builds a cross-partner profile neither partner authorised.
questions.l1: No Art. 12 controls; intermediary operations are commingled, data may be reused for other purposes, and evidence is missing
questions.l2: Neutrality is stated in policy, but intermediary and commercial workloads share databases and staff access.
questions.l3: Some neutrality/separation controls exist, but segregation, security measures, and audit evidence are incomplete or inconsistently enforced across services/partners
questions.l4: Separation, security measures and monitoring are enforced across services, but evidence bundles or periodic attestations are incomplete for some partners.
questions.l5: Full Art. 12 implementation with enforced non-use constraints, operational separation, technical/organizational controls, continuous monitoring, and audit-ready evidence bundles aligned to competent authority expectations
questions.remediation: Run intermediation workloads in a separate tenant with distinct credentials, and alert when any principal from the commercial side reads intermediation storage.
questions.text: If the agent provides data intermediation services, does it operationalize DGA Art. 12 by enforcing neutrality and separation (no data use for other purposes, ring-fenced operations), implementing appropriate technical and organizational measures for secure intermediation, and maintaining audit-ready evidence (policies, access logs, segregation controls, and periodic compliance attestations)?

questions.failureMode: The agent iterates object ids in a partner API call and retrieves records belonging to other tenants because ownership is never checked.
questions.l1: No object-level authorization; endpoints rely on client-provided identifiers without ownership/tenant checks and lack authorization tests
questions.l2: Ownership checks are coded in a few handlers; other endpoints trust the object id in the request.
questions.l3: Implements some object/tenant checks, but coverage is inconsistent, authorization logic is duplicated, or test evidence is incomplete
questions.l4: Centralised authorisation covers every object access with per-endpoint tests, but decision logs lack the fields needed to reconstruct an incident.
questions.l5: Full API1 prevention with centralized authorization, consistent ownership/tenant checks, automated authZ test suites per endpoint/resource, and audit-ready access decision logs
questions.remediation: Move object ownership and tenant checks into one policy enforcement point, add negative tests requesting another tenant's object ids, and log every decision.
questions.text: Does the agent prevent OWASP API1 (Broken Object Level Authorization) by enforcing object ownership/tenant isolation on every object access, using centralized authorization (policy enforcement points), and maintaining automated authorization test coverage (positive/negative cases) with logs suitable for incident reconstruction?

questions.failureMode: The agent queues a user's data access request behind batch jobs for weeks and nothing records the delay.
questions.l1: Access is ad hoc/manual; interfaces are insecure or slow, and timeliness/continuity evidence is missing
questions.l2: Access is granted through manual extracts, with no record of when a request was fulfilled.
questions.l3: Access interfaces exist, but timeliness/continuity SLAs and evidence are incomplete or inconsistently met
questions.l4: Secure interfaces with SLA monitoring exist, but continuity of access is not evidenced or SLA misses carry no recorded reason.
questions.l5: Full Art. 4 operationalization with secure interfaces, timeliness/continuity controls, SLA monitoring, and audit-ready access evidence bundles
questions.remediation: Instrument the access interface with per-request fulfilment timestamps and an SLA alert, and keep the audit log as evidence of no undue delay.
questions.text: Does the agent implement EU Data Act Art. 4 access obligations in an operationally usable way (secure access interface, timely/continuous access where applicable, SLA evidence for no undue delay, and audit logs proving access was provided to users upon request)?

questions.failureMode: The agent stores customer data in a proprietary format with no tested export, so a customer attempting to switch is effectively locked in.
questions.l1: No switching support and no switching terms in the contract.
questions.l2: Data export exists, but the contract is silent on switching rights.
questions.l3: Contract states switching rights and export is possible, but switching charges remain planned after 12 January 2027 or no exit has been exercised in a test.
questions.l4: Written switching terms exist and exit to another provider is tested, but exit to on-premises is untested or switching charges are not yet zero in billing.
questions.l5: Written switching terms provided before contract signature; exit to another provider and to on-premises tested with records; switching charges set to zero from 12 January 2027 with billing evidence.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU Data Act Art. 23; EU Data Act Art. 25(1); EU Data Act Art. 29(1)
questions.remediation: Run a timed exit test that moves a customer workload from the agent's platform to another provider and to on-premises, recording data completeness.
questions.text: If the agent provides or brokers data processing services, does it enable customers to switch to another provider or to on-premises infrastructure under a written contract that sets out switching rights (EU Data Act Arts. 23, 25(1)), and impose no switching charges from 12 January 2027 (Art. 29(1))?

questions.failureMode: The agent, as a data recipient, uses product data shared for a repair service to train a pricing model outside the purpose the user agreed.
questions.l1: No path to share user data with user-designated third parties.
questions.l2: Third-party sharing happens through bespoke engineering requests with no standard path.
questions.l3: Sharing happens on request, but recipient-side limits under Art. 6 are not enforced or recorded.
questions.l4: Self-service sharing with technical purpose restriction exists, but recipient-side use is not fully logged.
questions.l5: Self-service sharing to user-designated recipients; recipient use restricted to the agreed purpose with technical enforcement; every share and recipient use logged.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU Data Act Art. 5; EU Data Act Art. 6
questions.remediation: When the agent receives Data Act data as a recipient, tag it with the agreed purpose and block any query or model training outside that purpose.
questions.text: When a user asks for product or related-service data to be shared with a third party, does the agent make it available to that third party (EU Data Act Art. 5) and, when the agent is the recipient, use the data only within the limits of Art. 6?

questions.failureMode: The agent answers a request to know with category summaries and omits the inferred profile it built by correlating ecosystem data.
questions.l1: Responses to requests to know are not machine-readable.
questions.l2: Responses list categories in prose; specific pieces of personal information are not returned.
questions.l3: Machine-readable responses for some categories; transmission to another entity not supported.
questions.l4: All specific pieces are returned machine-readably, but transmission to another entity is not available on request.
questions.l5: All specific pieces returned in a structured machine-readable format; transmission to another entity on request; request handling logged with response dates.
questions.remediation: Generate request-to-know responses from the data inventory as structured JSON listing every specific piece, and offer transmission to an entity the consumer names.
questions.text: On a verifiable consumer request to know, does the business provide the specific pieces of personal information in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format that can be transmitted to another entity, to the extent technically feasible (Cal. Civ. Code §1798.130(a)(3)(B)(iii))?

questions.failureMode: The agent wires in a new partner connector on its own, and that supplier's compromise opens a path into the operator's network.
questions.l1: No supplier security assessment for ecosystem integrations.
questions.l2: Ecosystem suppliers are listed, but none has a security assessment.
questions.l3: Supplier inventory with security assessment for critical suppliers only; no contractual security requirements or re-assessment trigger.
questions.l4: Every supplier is assessed with contractual security clauses, but re-assessment on change or incident is not triggered.
questions.l5: Every direct supplier and service provider in the ecosystem inventoried with a security assessment, contractual security clauses and re-assessment on change or incident; evidence retained.
questions.remediation: Block the agent from adding an ecosystem integration until the supplier has a security assessment, and re-assess on supplier incident or major change.
questions.text: Where the operator is an essential or important entity under NIS2, does the agent's ecosystem integration apply supply chain security measures covering the security of relationships with direct suppliers and service providers (Directive (EU) 2022/2555 Art. 21(2)(d))?

questions.failureMode: The agent co-builds an audience segment with a partner, and a data subject's access request bounces between both because neither holds responsibility.
questions.l1: Joint processing with partners is not identified and no arrangement exists.
questions.l2: Partners are treated as processors by default; joint processing is never identified.
questions.l3: Joint processing is identified and arrangements exist for some partners, or arrangements do not allocate responsibility for data subject rights and Art. 13-14 information.
questions.l4: Every joint-controller relationship has an arrangement and contact point, but arrangements are not reviewed when the joint processing changes.
questions.l5: Every joint-controller relationship in the ecosystem is inventoried with an arrangement allocating rights handling and Art. 13-14 information duties and naming a contact point for data subjects; arrangements are reviewed whenever the joint processing changes, with review records.
questions.remediation: Flag any agent workflow that combines personal data with a partner for a shared purpose and require an Art. 26 arrangement id before it runs.
questions.text: Where the agent's operator and ecosystem partners jointly determine the purposes and means of processing personal data, have they set out their respective responsibilities, in particular for data subject rights and the information duties of Arts. 13 and 14, in an arrangement between them (GDPR Art. 26(1))?

questions.failureMode: The agent offers a dataset to data-space participants with no licence or quality metadata, so automated consumers ingest it under the wrong use restriction.
questions.l1: Data offered to data-space participants without machine-readable dataset descriptions or API descriptions.
questions.l2: Offered datasets are described on marketing pages only; there is no machine-readable metadata.
questions.l3: Dataset or API descriptions exist for some offerings, or omit licences, data quality or terms of use.
questions.l4: Machine-readable descriptions exist for every dataset and access API, but they are not validated on each release.
questions.l5: Every offered dataset has a machine-readable description covering content, use restrictions, licence, collection methodology and quality; every access API is described with its terms of use and quality of service; descriptions are validated on each release.
questions.remediation: Publish a machine-readable description for each offered dataset and access API, including licence, quality and terms of use, and validate it in the release pipeline.
questions.text: Where the agent's operator offers data or data services to other participants in a data space, does it describe dataset content, use restrictions, licences, collection methodology and quality in a machine-readable format, and describe its access APIs with their terms of use and quality of service sufficiently to enable automatic access (EU Data Act Art. 33(1)(a), (c))?

regulatoryReferences.citation: California Consumer Privacy Act as amended by CPRA (Cal. Civ. Code §1798.100 et seq.) and CPPA regulations
ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Information security management systems (with Amd 1:2024)

no-poverty.certificationPath: L1 Basic financial access provision → L2 Responsible lending with consumer protection → L3 Full financial inclusion with CGAP standards → L4 AI-enhanced poverty reduction with impact measurement → L5 Autonomous inclusive finance governance with verified poverty reduction outcomes
no-poverty.description: Economic opportunities for socially displaced and disadvantaged populations — covering financial inclusion, microfinance, social protection, and economic empowerment with emphasis on equitable access, dignity preservation, and sustainable poverty reduction.
no-poverty.euAIActClassification: Annex III §5(a) — public assistance benefits and services; §5(b) — creditworthiness of natural persons
keyRisks: Predatory lending through AI-optimized high-interest microloans
Financial exclusion reinforcement through biased credit algorithms
Dignity violation through invasive poverty verification processes
Data exploitation of vulnerable population financial behavior
Debt trap creation through AI-managed lending without affordability assessment
no-poverty.name: No Poverty

questions.failureMode: The agent pushes a top-up microloan to a borrower already repaying three other lenders because its objective rewards disbursement volume.
questions.l1: No predatory lending prevention; AI lending algorithms optimize for revenue without affordability assessment or interest rate caps
questions.l2: Interest rates are reported to management, but loan offers are not checked for affordability before the agent makes them
questions.l3: Agent implements basic affordability checks and interest rate monitoring, but does not assess cumulative debt burden or prevent over-indebtedness across multiple lenders
questions.l4: Affordability, cumulative debt burden across lenders and pricing fairness are assessed, but collection practices are not monitored
questions.l5: Comprehensive predatory lending prevention with affordability assessment, cumulative debt burden analysis, interest rate fairness evaluation, transparent pricing disclosure, over-indebtedness early warning, and responsible collection practices per CGAP principles
questions.remediation: Make the loan-offer tool refuse an offer until an affordability check including credit-bureau debt across lenders is recorded, and cap the price the agent can propose per product.
questions.text: Does the agent prevent predatory lending per the CGAP Client Protection Principles?

questions.failureMode: The agent rejects a refugee's account application because the identity document type is missing from its accepted-ID list.
questions.l1: No inclusion assessment; financial services algorithms may exclude displaced populations, refugees, or undocumented individuals
questions.l2: Exclusion is noticed only through complaints from refugee or displaced applicants
questions.l3: Agent tracks service access metrics by population segment and flags exclusion patterns, but does not implement alternative identification or credit assessment for underserved populations
questions.l4: Alternative ID and non-traditional credit assessment are accepted, but inclusion outcomes are not measured by population segment
questions.l5: Full financial inclusion with alternative ID acceptance per UNHCR guidelines, non-traditional credit assessment, refugee/displaced population accommodation, language accessibility, cultural sensitivity, and inclusion impact measurement
questions.remediation: Accept the alternative identity documents listed for displaced populations in the onboarding tool, and alert when approval rates for refugee applicants drop below the overall rate.
questions.text: Does the agent ensure financial inclusion without discrimination for refugees and displaced people per the UNHCR guidelines on financial inclusion?

questions.failureMode: The agent demands a utility bill and payslip from a customer opening a capped basic wallet, so a low-income applicant abandons onboarding.
questions.l1: No simplified CDD; all customers face the same due diligence requirements regardless of risk level, creating barriers for low-income populations
questions.l2: Low-risk products are named in policy, but every customer still goes through full due diligence
questions.l3: Agent applies tiered CDD based on product risk level, but simplified procedures are not systematically designed for financial inclusion or aligned with FATF guidance
questions.l4: Simplified due diligence with tiered limits and progressive KYC is applied, but the risk assessment justifying it is not documented
questions.l5: Risk-based CDD with FATF-aligned simplified procedures for low-risk inclusion products, tiered account limits, progressive KYC as usage increases, and documented risk assessment justifying simplified measures per FATF R1 and inclusion guidance
questions.regulatoryRef: FATF Recommendation 1; FATF Guidance on Financial Inclusion (2017)
questions.remediation: Encode tiered account limits per product risk level and make the agent request additional KYC only when a customer's usage crosses the tier limit.
questions.text: Does the agent implement simplified due diligence per FATF Recommendation 1 risk-based approach for low-risk financial inclusion products?

questions.failureMode: The agent completes a transfer to a scammer posing as a support line because the low-literacy user confirmed a text prompt they could not read.
questions.l1: No mobile money security; digital financial services lack fraud protection appropriate for vulnerable and low-literacy users
questions.l2: Transactions are PIN-protected, but no fraud alerting or scam warning exists for users
questions.l3: Agent implements basic transaction security and fraud alerts, but user interfaces are not designed for low-literacy users and fraud education is not provided
questions.l4: Low-literacy UI, voice confirmation and local-language scam warnings are in place, but agent-network fraud is not monitored
questions.l5: Comprehensive mobile money security with low-literacy UI design, voice-based transaction confirmation, fraud education in local languages, social engineering protection, agent network fraud monitoring, and GSMA certification compliance
questions.regulatoryRef: GSMA Mobile Money Certification; GSMA Code of Conduct for Mobile Money
questions.remediation: Add voice read-back of amount and recipient before the agent completes a mobile money transfer, and monitor cash-agent float patterns for fraud with an alert threshold.
questions.text: Does the agent implement mobile money security per GSMA Mobile Money Certification requirements and protect low-literacy users from fraud?

questions.failureMode: The agent quotes a flat weekly fee that the borrower cannot translate into an annual cost, and records the sign-up as informed consent.
questions.l1: No financial literacy support; product terms are presented in complex language without educational context
questions.l2: Product terms are simplified on paper, but the agent presents them in the same complex language
questions.l3: Agent provides simplified product information and basic financial literacy content, but does not personalize education or assess user comprehension
questions.l4: Personalised explanations with visual and audio formats are given, but user comprehension is not checked before the agent accepts a sign-up
questions.l5: Full financial literacy integration with personalized education, comprehension verification, transparent product comparison, total cost disclosure in local currency, visual/audio explanations for low-literacy users, and ongoing financial capability building
questions.regulatoryRef: World Bank FCP Good Practices Principle 3
questions.remediation: Ask the customer to restate the total repayment amount in local currency before the agent accepts the loan, and re-explain in voice if the answer is wrong.
questions.text: Does the agent provide financial literacy support and transparent product information per World Bank Good Practices Principle 3 (Disclosure and Transparency)?

questions.failureMode: The agent reports growth in loans disbursed as success while the same cohort's repayment stress and asset sales rise unseen.
questions.l1: No impact measurement; financial inclusion activities are not assessed for actual poverty reduction outcomes
questions.l2: Outputs such as accounts opened are reported, with no baseline of client income or poverty status
questions.l3: Agent tracks basic financial access metrics (accounts opened, loans disbursed) but does not measure poverty reduction outcomes or economic empowerment indicators
questions.l4: Income change, resilience and multidimensional poverty indicators are tracked over time, but results are not published or used to adjust products
questions.l5: Comprehensive impact measurement with SDG 1 indicator tracking, income improvement measurement, economic resilience assessment, multidimensional poverty index integration, longitudinal outcome tracking, and transparent impact reporting
questions.regulatoryRef: UN SDG 1 Indicators 1.1.1, 1.2.1; World Bank Poverty Measurement
questions.remediation: Record a poverty baseline per client at onboarding and track repayment stress and income change per cohort, pausing a product when the stress indicator crosses a threshold.
questions.text: Does the agent measure poverty reduction impact per UN SDG 1 indicators and World Bank poverty measurement methodology?

questions.failureMode: The agent uses a borrower's disclosed medical condition, given for a hardship request, as a feature in a later credit decision.
questions.l1: No vulnerable population data protection; financial data of displaced/disadvantaged populations is processed without enhanced safeguards
questions.l2: Customer data is encrypted, but special-category data such as health or ethnicity flows into the agent like any other field
questions.l3: Agent applies basic data protection to all customer data, but does not implement enhanced protections for special-category data of vulnerable populations
questions.l4: Special-category data is minimised and purpose-limited with explicit consent, but re-identification risk is not assessed before sharing
questions.l5: Full vulnerable population data protection with enhanced consent processes, data minimization, purpose limitation, re-identification risk assessment, and data sharing restrictions for special-category data
questions.remediation: Tag special-category fields and strip them from the agent's context unless a recorded explicit-consent purpose covers the task.
questions.text: Does the agent protect vulnerable population data per GDPR Article 9 special category protections?

questions.failureMode: The agent optimises loan officer routes for disbursement volume, steering away from the poorest villages the institution claims to serve.
questions.l1: No social performance tracking; financial inclusion operations are not assessed against social performance standards
questions.l2: Outreach to women and rural clients is counted, but staff and agent incentives reward volume only
questions.l3: Agent tracks basic social metrics (outreach to poor, women, rural populations) but does not implement full social performance management or client outcome monitoring
questions.l4: Client outcomes are monitored and pricing is checked, but staff and agent incentive alignment with social goals is not evidenced
questions.l5: Comprehensive SPM with CERISE-SPTF standard implementation, client outcome monitoring, social audit readiness, responsible pricing verification, staff incentive alignment with social goals, and transparent social performance reporting
questions.remediation: Add client-outcome measures (repayment stress, dropout) to the agent's objective alongside volume, and report them in the social performance dashboard.
questions.text: Does the agent maintain social performance management per CERISE-SPTF Universal Standards for Social Performance Management?

questions.failureMode: The agent sends a thin-file applicant a denial citing late payments that do not exist, because reasons come from a fixed template.
questions.l1: Notices give no reasons or only that the applicant did not reach a qualifying score
questions.l2: Notices give generic reasons such as insufficient credit history for every denial
questions.l3: Reasons come from a fixed list that is not tied to the features the model used for that applicant
questions.l4: Reasons are computed per decision from model attributions, but are not checked against the decision record before the notice is sent
questions.l5: Reasons are computed per decision from the model's attributions, checked for accuracy against the decision record, and retained with it
questions.remediation: Derive the principal reasons for each denial from the model's attributions for that applicant, check them against the decision record, and retain both with the notice.
questions.text: For every US credit denial or other adverse action the agent decides or supports, does the notice state the specific principal reasons derived from the model features actually used (12 CFR 1002.9(b)(2)), in a format accessible to applicants without credit history?

questions.failureMode: The agent starts using phone top-up frequency in credit decisions, which tracks national origin, with no proxy test.
questions.l1: Alternative-data sources are added without proxy testing
questions.l2: Alternative-data sources are reviewed informally when added, with no recorded proxy test
questions.l3: Sources are proxy-tested when first added, but not re-tested when the source or model changes
questions.l4: Each source is proxy-tested before use and on change, but failing sources are not blocked automatically
questions.l5: Every alternative-data source has a recorded proxy test before use and on each change, failing sources are blocked, and the record is retained with the model version
questions.remediation: Require a recorded proxy test before the agent's feature store accepts a new alternative-data source, and block any source that fails on re-test.
questions.text: Before an alternative-data source (mobile, utility, social or transaction data) is used in credit decisions for underserved applicants, is it tested for acting as a proxy for a prohibited basis under 12 CFR 1002.6(b), with the result recorded?

questions.failureMode: The agent's marketing targeting quietly excludes low- and moderate-income tracts because response rates there are lower.
questions.l1: No CRA support; no assessment area mapping, LMI outcome measurement, or exam-ready evidence of qualifying activities
questions.l2: Lending to low- and moderate-income areas is reported ad hoc, with no assessment-area mapping
questions.l3: Tracks some LMI outreach and lending metrics, but assessment area alignment and evidence packaging for CRA exams are incomplete
questions.l4: Assessment areas and LMI outcomes are tracked, but qualifying activities are not tagged or bundled for examination
questions.l5: Full CRA readiness with assessment-area mapping, LMI outcome dashboards, qualifying activity tagging, exam-ready evidence bundles, and governance reporting aligned to CRA performance context
questions.regulatoryRef: Community Reinvestment Act (CRA) — community reinvestment and LMI outcomes
questions.remediation: Tag each loan and outreach action the agent takes with its assessment area and LMI status, and alert when the agent's targeting shifts volume away from LMI tracts.
questions.text: If the provider is subject to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA), does the agent support CRA-aligned community reinvestment by (1) mapping products and outreach to assessment areas, (2) measuring lending/service outcomes to low- and moderate-income (LMI) communities, and (3) producing examination-ready evidence of qualifying activities and impact?

questions.failureMode: The agent sells a savings-linked insurance add-on to a daily-wage user who cannot sustain the premium, and the complaint sits unanswered.
questions.l1: No GPFI-aligned DFS controls; suitability, dispute resolution, and scam resilience are not systematically implemented
questions.l2: Disclosures exist and complaints are taken by phone, but suitability is not checked and resolution times are not measured
questions.l3: Implements some disclosures and basic complaints intake, but suitability checks, resolution SLAs, and scam/fraud resilience are incomplete
questions.l4: Suitability gating, total-cost disclosure and complaint SLAs are monitored, but scam-resilience measures are not tested with low-literacy users
questions.l5: Full GPFI-aligned DFS consumer outcomes with suitability gating, total-cost transparency, monitored complaint/dispute SLAs, scam resilience patterns, and auditable reporting of consumer harm reduction
questions.regulatoryRef: World Bank GPFI (2020) — responsible DFS / consumer protection
questions.remediation: Add a suitability check that stops the agent offering a product outside a vulnerable user's profile, and time every complaint against a resolution SLA with breach alerts.
questions.text: Does the agent implement World Bank / GPFI 2020-aligned responsible DFS controls, including product suitability checks for vulnerable users, transparent total cost disclosures, accessible complaints + dispute resolution SLAs, and fraud/scam resilience (social engineering protections) for low-literacy populations?

questions.failureMode: The agent-run simplified-account channel suffers repeated cash-out fraud that is never recorded as a channel incident.
questions.l1: No documented risk controls for the inclusion channel
questions.l2: Risk controls for the inclusion channel are informal and differ by region
questions.l3: Controls are documented, but channel incidents are not recorded or not reported to the board
questions.l4: Controls are documented and incidents recorded, but board reporting on channel risk is irregular
questions.l5: Controls are documented with a proportionality rationale, every channel incident is recorded, and board reports on channel risk are evidenced at the defined cadence
questions.regulatoryRef: BCBS Guidance on the application of the Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision to institutions relevant to financial inclusion (2016)
questions.remediation: Log every incident in the agent-run inclusion channel against a documented control and produce a channel-risk report for the board at the defined cadence.
questions.text: Does the operator of the agent-run inclusion channel (simplified accounts, agent networks) apply documented proportional risk controls, record incidents from that channel, and report channel risk to the board at a defined cadence?

questions.failureMode: The agent approves a program-funded microloan for an ineligible applicant because the program's eligibility rules were never encoded.
questions.l1: No EU microfinance compliance support; obligations are not recognized or documented
questions.l2: EU microfinance obligations are known to the compliance team, but are not mapped to the agent's workflows
questions.l3: Recognizes EU microfinance obligations at a policy level, but implementation controls and evidence outputs are incomplete
questions.l4: Obligations are mapped to controlled workflows, but reporting outputs for program administrators are produced manually
questions.l5: Full EU microfinance compliance with obligation mapping, controlled workflows, reporting outputs, and audit-ready evidence for §3 requirements
questions.remediation: Map each EU microfinance obligation to a check in the agent's loan workflow, and generate the program report from the logged checks.
questions.text: For EU microfinance programs, does the agent comply with EU Microfinance Reg §3 requirements (eligibility / conduct obligations as applicable), including customer protections, reporting evidence, and audit-ready documentation for program administrators/supervisors?

questions.failureMode: The agent's new voice onboarding channel goes live with full-KYC rules copied from branch banking, rejecting the unbanked users it targets.
questions.l1: New agent-driven channels launch with no ML/TF risk assessment
questions.l2: ML/TF risk is discussed at launch, but no assessment is recorded
questions.l3: A risk assessment is done at launch, but it is not repeated when the agent's behaviour, channel or customer segment changes
questions.l4: Assessments are recorded and re-run on material change, but control calibration is not checked for excluding low-risk customers
questions.l5: Pre-launch ML/TF assessment with documented mitigations, re-run on material changes to the agent or channel, calibrated so controls stay proportionate and do not exclude low-risk customers
questions.remediation: Re-run the ML/TF assessment whenever the agent's behaviour, channel or customer segment changes, and measure how many low-risk applicants each new control rejects.
questions.text: Before launching an agent-driven product, delivery channel or technology for low-income or unbanked customers, does the provider assess and mitigate its money-laundering and terrorist-financing risks as FATF Recommendation 15 requires?

questions.failureMode: The agent grants a buy-now-pay-later line on a high bureau score while the consumer's bank data shows income below essential spending.
questions.l1: Credit can be granted without a recorded creditworthiness assessment
questions.l2: A credit score is checked before granting credit, but nothing measures whether the consumer can repay
questions.l3: An assessment is recorded, but it uses only lender-risk factors and no measure of the consumer's ability to repay
questions.l4: Ability to repay is assessed before every grant, but data sources are not recorded or declined-for-affordability outcomes are not retained
questions.l5: Every grant is blocked until an assessment of the consumer's ability to repay is recorded with its data sources, and declined-for-affordability outcomes are retained
questions.remediation: Block the credit grant tool until an ability-to-repay assessment with its income and expense data sources is recorded for the consumer.
questions.text: Before credit is granted to an EU consumer, does the agent complete and record a creditworthiness assessment carried out in the consumer's interest to prevent irresponsible lending and over-indebtedness (Directive (EU) 2023/2225 Art. 18(1))?

questions.failureMode: The agent answers a consumer's request for human review of a declined loan by restating the score, and the request is never routed.
questions.l1: No route to human intervention or explanation
questions.l2: Consumers can complain about an automated decision, but there is no defined route to human intervention
questions.l3: Human intervention is available on request, but explanations are generic or contests are not recorded
questions.l4: Human intervention, explanation and contest are available and logged, but response times are not tracked
questions.l5: Each automated assessment can be explained from its record, requests for human intervention and contests are logged with outcomes and response times
questions.remediation: Add a human-review request option to every automated creditworthiness result, generate the explanation from the assessment record, and log each contest with outcome and response time.
questions.text: Where the creditworthiness assessment uses automated processing, can the consumer request and obtain human intervention, a clear explanation of the assessment and its logic, and to express a view and contest the decision (Directive (EU) 2023/2225 Art. 18(8))?

questions.failureMode: The agent supplies a probability-of-default score that lenders use as a hard cut-off, while the operator treats it as mere advice.
questions.l1: Scores are supplied without an Art. 22 assessment
questions.l2: Lenders' reliance on the score is known informally, but no Art. 22 assessment exists
questions.l3: An Art. 22 basis is recorded, but safeguards (human intervention, contest) are not available to data subjects
questions.l4: The Art. 22(2) basis is recorded and safeguards are offered, but the assessment is not revisited when lenders' use of the score changes
questions.l5: The Art. 22(2) basis is recorded per use case, safeguards are offered and their use is logged, and the assessment is reviewed when the score's use by lenders changes
questions.remediation: Record the Art. 22(2) basis for each lender use of the score, expose human intervention and contest routes to data subjects, and reopen the record when a lender changes how it uses the score.
questions.text: If the agent produces a credit-score or probability value that lenders draw on strongly to grant or refuse credit, does the operator treat it as automated individual decision-making under GDPR Art. 22 (per CJEU C-634/21), with a recorded Art. 22(2) basis and safeguards?

questions.failureMode: The agent attaches a list of refugee cash-transfer recipients with locations to a donor report it drafts, exposing  them to re-identification.
questions.l1: Data about humanitarian beneficiaries is processed like any other customer data
questions.l2: Beneficiary data is labelled sensitive, but no minimisation or purpose review is done for agent data flows
questions.l3: Minimisation and purpose limits are documented, but sharing with third parties (including authorities and donors) is not restricted or recorded
questions.l4: Purpose and minimisation are reviewed per flow and third-party sharing requires an assessment, but re-identification risk is not assessed before releases
questions.l5: Each beneficiary data flow has a recorded purpose and minimisation review, sharing with any third party requires a documented assessment, and re-identification risk is assessed before any release
questions.regulatoryRef: ICRC Handbook on Data Protection in Humanitarian Action
questions.remediation: Require a recorded sharing assessment before the agent's tools can export beneficiary data to any third party, including donors and authorities.
questions.text: Where the agent processes data about refugees, displaced people or other recipients of humanitarian assistance, does it apply the data protection principles of the ICRC Handbook on Data Protection in Humanitarian Action, including limits on sharing with third parties?

regulatoryReferences.citation: IFC Performance Standards on Environmental and Social Sustainability
UNHCR guidance on financial inclusion of refugees
EU microfinance citation as written in pack content

sdgAlignment: SDG 8 — Decent Work and Economic Growth

os-sustainable-outcomes.certificationPath: L1 Basic operational monitoring → L2 ITIL/ISO 20000 service management → L3 SOC 2 + ISO 27001 certified → L4 DORA compliant resilience → L5 Autonomous sustainable orchestration with verified outcomes and continuous accountability
os-sustainable-outcomes.description: The transactional system orchestrating strategic movement of people, goods, and money — creating wealth and value while enabling sustainable outcomes — AI agents as the core orchestration layer for economic and social systems with resilience, accountability, and outcome measurement.
os-sustainable-outcomes.euAIActClassification: Annex III §2 (critical digital infrastructure) and §4 (workers' management) where those uses apply
keyRisks: Systemic failure propagation through interconnected orchestration failures
Accountability gaps in AI-mediated economic transactions
Inequitable outcome distribution amplified by algorithmic optimization
Regulatory arbitrage enabled by multi-jurisdiction AI orchestration
Operational resilience failures in critical transaction pathways
os-sustainable-outcomes.name: Operating System for Sustainable Outcomes

questions.failureMode: The agent's tool router reaches payment rails through a path outside the ICT risk framework, so a compromise there goes unmonitored.
questions.l1: No documented ICT risk management framework covering the orchestration system.
questions.l2: An ICT risk framework exists for the wider entity but does not name the agent orchestration layer.
questions.l3: Framework documented and covers the orchestration system, but Art. 9 protection and prevention measures are not mapped to the agent's components.
questions.l4: Art. 9 measures are mapped per component with owners, but the framework was not reviewed after the last major ICT-related incident.
questions.l5: Framework covers the agent orchestration layer; Art. 9 measures mapped per component with owners; framework reviewed on a documented schedule and after major ICT-related incidents, with review records.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU DORA Art. 6; EU DORA Art. 9
questions.remediation: List each orchestration component (planner, tool router, payment connectors) in the ICT risk framework and map Art. 9 protection measures to it with an owner.
questions.text: For financial-sector orchestration in DORA scope, does the agent operate within a documented ICT risk management framework (EU DORA Art. 6) with protection and prevention measures (Art. 9)?

questions.failureMode: The agent changes a routing rule in a live orchestration service without a change record, and the resulting SLA breach cannot be traced to its cause.
questions.l1: No service catalogue, SLAs or change records for orchestration services.
questions.l2: Orchestration services run without catalogue entries; incidents are handled in chat with no records.
questions.l3: Service catalogue, SLAs, incident and change records exist, but SLA attainment is not reported or improvement actions are not tracked.
questions.l4: Catalogue, SLAs and monthly attainment reports exist, but incident, problem and change records are not linked or improvement actions stall.
questions.l5: Every orchestration service is in the catalogue with SLAs; SLA attainment is reported monthly; incident, problem and change records are linked; improvement actions are tracked to closure.
questions.remediation: Register each agent-run orchestration service in the catalogue with an SLA, and require every agent-initiated change to carry a change record linked to the service.
questions.text: Does the agent maintain service management per ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018 §8 service delivery requirements?

questions.failureMode: The agent's service account holds standing production access outside the SOC 2 scope, so its privileged changes are never reviewed.
questions.l1: No mapping of controls to TSC CC6-CC9 and no SOC 2 report.
questions.l2: Access controls exist but are not mapped to the TSC, and no auditor has examined the agent.
questions.l3: Controls mapped to CC6-CC7 with evidence; CC8 change management or CC9 risk mitigation controls are unmapped, or no Type II report covers the agent.
questions.l4: CC6-CC9 are mapped with automated evidence and a Type II report exists, but its system description omits the agent layer or exceptions remain open.
questions.l5: Controls mapped to CC6-CC9 with automated evidence collection; a current SOC 2 Type II report whose system description includes the agent orchestration layer; exceptions remediated with records.
questions.remediation: Bring the agent's service accounts, tool permissions and change pipeline into the SOC 2 system description and collect CC6-CC9 evidence for them automatically.
questions.text: Does the agent implement security operations per SOC 2 Type II Trust Service Criteria CC6-CC9 logical and physical access controls and system operations?

questions.failureMode: The agent optimises routing for lowest cost and quietly shifts delays onto rural customers because only efficiency is measured.
questions.l1: No outcome accountability; orchestration system optimizes for efficiency without measuring or reporting social and economic outcomes
questions.l2: Only throughput and cost metrics are tracked; no economic or social outcome measures exist.
questions.l3: Agent tracks economic performance metrics and generates basic GRI-aligned reports, but does not implement full SDG impact measurement or stakeholder outcome reporting
questions.l4: GRI 201-207 reporting and SDG impact measurement are in place, but stakeholder outcome distribution or negative externalities are not analysed.
questions.l5: Full outcome accountability with GRI 201-207 economic reporting, UN SDG impact measurement per SDG Impact Standards, stakeholder outcome distribution analysis, negative externality identification, and transparent sustainable outcome reporting
questions.regulatoryRef: GRI Standards 201-207; UN SDG Impact Standards
questions.remediation: Add outcome metrics per stakeholder group beside efficiency metrics in the orchestration objective, and report the negative externalities the optimisation produces.
questions.text: Does the agent implement outcome accountability per GRI Standards 201-207 economic performance reporting and UN SDG impact measurement framework?

questions.failureMode: The agent resumes after a state-store failover from a snapshot hours old and replays payment instructions that had already settled.
questions.l1: No business impact analysis and no RTO/RPO for orchestration pathways.
questions.l2: Backups exist, but there is no business impact analysis and no RTO or RPO for orchestration pathways.
questions.l3: RTO/RPO set and continuity plans documented for core pathways, but exercises do not measure achieved recovery times or some critical pathways are not covered.
questions.l4: The BIA covers every critical pathway and exercises measure achieved RTO/RPO, but gaps found in exercises are not tracked to closure.
questions.l5: Business impact analysis covers every critical pathway; documented recovery procedures; exercises at least annually measure achieved RTO/RPO against targets; gaps tracked to closure.
questions.remediation: Set RTO and RPO for each critical orchestration pathway in the BIA and run a failover exercise that measures achieved recovery time against them.
questions.text: Does the agent implement business continuity per ISO 22301:2019 §8.4 business continuity plans with RTO/RPO verification for critical orchestration pathways?

questions.failureMode: The agent's allocation policy gives one region systematically slower service and no disparity metric surfaces it.
questions.l1: No measurement of access or outcome disparities across user groups.
questions.l2: Complaints about unequal service are handled one by one; no disparity metric exists.
questions.l3: Disparities measured for some groups or ad hoc, without documented thresholds or remediation.
questions.l4: Disparity metrics and thresholds run on schedule with tracked remediation, but results are not reported to stakeholders.
questions.l5: Disparity metrics per defined group on a fixed schedule; thresholds documented; each breach triggers tracked remediation; results reported to stakeholders.
questions.regulatoryRef: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (2021): Fairness and non-discrimination
questions.remediation: Compute access and outcome rates per defined user group weekly from orchestration logs and open a remediation ticket whenever a gap exceeds the documented threshold.
questions.text: Does the agent measure disparities in access to and outcomes of its orchestration services across defined user groups and act on them, per the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI principle 'Fairness and non-discrimination'?

questions.failureMode: The agent's orchestration network has no segmentation, so one compromised connector propagates to every downstream transaction system.
questions.l1: No NIS2 cybersecurity measures; orchestration system does not implement essential entity security requirements per Art. 21
questions.l2: A few security measures (backups, MFA) exist with no mapping to Art. 21.
questions.l3: Agent implements several Art. 21 security measures including incident handling and supply chain security, but does not address all required measures
questions.l4: Most Art. 21 measures are in place with regular testing, but at least one, such as cryptography or supply chain, lacks evidence for the orchestration system.
questions.l5: Full NIS2 compliance with all Art. 21 measures, 24-hour incident notification capability, supply chain security, cryptographic controls, access control, and regular cybersecurity testing per Art. 21(2)(i)
questions.remediation: Build an Art. 21(2) coverage matrix for the orchestration system with one evidence link per measure, and schedule recurring security tests of the agent's tool interfaces.
questions.text: Does the agent implement NIS2 cybersecurity measures per EU NIS2 Directive 2022/2555 Article 21 for essential entity digital infrastructure?

questions.failureMode: The agent starts sending customer data to a new third-country analytics tool that no record of processing entry mentions.
questions.l1: No record of processing activities, or agent-driven processing is absent from it.
questions.l2: The record of processing describes the product in general; new agent tools are added without updating it.
questions.l3: The record lists agent-driven processing, but at least one Art. 30(1)(b)-(g) item is missing for an activity, or the record was not updated after the last change to the agent's processing.
questions.l4: Every agent activity has a complete versioned entry, but the record is not reconciled against the processing inventory on schedule.
questions.l5: Every agent-driven processing activity has a record entry with each Art. 30(1) item; entries are versioned and updated on each change to the agent's processing; the record is reconciled against the agent's processing inventory on a documented schedule.
questions.remediation: Fail the deploy of any agent tool that processes personal data until a matching Art. 30 record entry exists, and reconcile entries against tool manifests monthly.
questions.text: Does the controller's record of processing activities (GDPR Art. 30(1)) cover every processing activity the agent performs, with its purposes, categories of data subjects and personal data, recipients, third-country transfers, erasure time limits and a description of security measures?

questions.failureMode: The agent's orchestration layer is carved out of TLPT, so no red team discovers that its tool router can be hijacked to move funds.
questions.l1: Agent orchestration layer excluded from resilience testing.
questions.l2: The orchestration layer receives only vulnerability scans and sits outside the resilience testing programme.
questions.l3: Orchestration layer covered by Art. 25 testing, but excluded from TLPT scope where TLPT is required, or tester qualifications not documented.
questions.l4: The layer is in the programme and in TLPT scope, but findings are not retested or tester requirements are only partly evidenced.
questions.l5: Orchestration layer in the testing programme and in TLPT scope; latest TLPT within 3 years; tester requirements evidenced; findings remediated and retested with records.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU DORA Art. 24; EU DORA Art. 25; EU DORA Art. 26; EU DORA Art. 27
questions.remediation: Add the agent orchestration environment, including its tool connectors, to the Art. 25 test plan and to TLPT scope, and retest each finding before closure.
questions.text: For financial entities in DORA scope, is the agent orchestration environment inside the digital operational resilience testing programme (EU DORA Arts. 24-25) and, where the entity must perform TLPT, inside threat-led penetration testing carried out at least every 3 years by testers meeting Art. 27 (Arts. 26-27)?

questions.failureMode: The agent is never attacked through agent-specific paths in red-team scenarios, so a prompt injection that drives its payment tools stays untested.
questions.l1: No TLPT: no threat-led testing program, no governance, and no evidence bundles
questions.l2: Annual penetration tests and occasional scenario exercises run, with no TLPT policy or independence controls.
questions.l3: Performs some penetration testing and occasional scenario exercises, but TLPT governance, independence, and evidence bundles are incomplete or not mapped to the required DORA anchor
questions.l4: TLPT policy, governance, threat-intelligence red teaming and remediation exist, but evidence bundles lack retest outcomes or rules of engagement.
questions.l5: Full TLPT program with governance, scoped threat-led testing, independence controls, remediation + retesting, and supervisor-ready evidence mapped to the required DORA Art. 9(4) anchor
questions.remediation: Write a TLPT policy whose scoping includes agent attack paths such as prompt injection driving tool calls, and assemble an evidence bundle per test with retests.
questions.text: Does the agent implement threat-led penetration testing (TLPT) governance and execution aligned to the Councils required mapping for EU DORA Art. 9(4), including (1) a TLPT policy and scoping methodology, (2) engagement governance and independence, (3) red-team execution with threat intelligence, (4) findings remediation tracking, and (5) an auditor/supervisor-ready evidence bundle (scope, rules of engagement, reports, remediation, and retest outcomes)?

questions.failureMode: The agent restores a customer database after an outage with permissions reset to open, exposing personal data that was access-controlled before.
questions.l1: No restore capability: backups/restores are undefined, untested, or cannot demonstrate timely restoration of availability/access
questions.l2: Backups run nightly but have never been restored in a drill.
questions.l3: Has backups and can restore in common cases, but restore drills, objectives, integrity verification, and evidence bundles are incomplete
questions.l4: Restore objectives and drills exist with integrity checks, but access restoration is not verified or drill evidence is not retained.
questions.l5: Full Art. 32(1)(c) readiness with defined restore objectives, regular restore testing, integrity and access verification, and audit-ready evidence bundles demonstrating timely restoration.
questions.remediation: Run a quarterly restore drill of each personal-data store the agent uses, verify checksums and access permissions after restore, and keep the drill report.
questions.text: Does the agent implement GDPR Art. 32(1)(c), the ability to restore the availability and access to personal data in a timely manner after a physical or technical incident, by maintaining (1) backup and restore procedures for personal-data processing systems, (2) restore time objectives and restore drills demonstrating timely restoration, (3) integrity checks and access restoration verification, and (4) evidence retention (logs, drill reports, corrective actions) suitable for supervisory authority review?

questions.failureMode: The agent keeps retrying failed downstream calls while humans recover from an outage, because no runbook step pauses it first.
questions.l1: No recovery procedures: BC plans are high-level and not executable, exercised, or evidenced
questions.l2: A high-level continuity plan exists; recovery steps live in individual engineers' heads.
questions.l3: Has recovery runbooks and exercises some scenarios, but invocation criteria, communications roles, and evidence bundles are incomplete
questions.l4: Executable runbooks with invocation criteria and roles are exercised, but after-action improvements are not fed back into the runbooks.
questions.l5: Full §8.4.4 compliance with executable recovery procedures, role/communication plans, regular exercises, after-action improvements, and auditor-ready evidence
questions.remediation: Write an executable runbook per critical orchestration pathway with invocation criteria, including how to pause the agent and drain its queue, and exercise it.
questions.text: Does the agent implement ISO 22301:2019 §8.4.4 recovery procedures by defining invocation criteria, step-by-step recovery runbooks for critical orchestration pathways, communications/roles during recovery, exercise/testing outputs, and evidence retention that demonstrates procedures are current and effective?

questions.failureMode: The agent depends on a single model endpoint that nobody mapped, and when it degrades every orchestration service fails at once.
questions.l1: No continuity or availability targets for orchestration services.
questions.l2: Availability is monitored for the front end only; dependencies are not mapped.
questions.l3: Targets set for some services; dependency mapping incomplete or plans not tested in the last 12 months.
questions.l4: Targets per service, mapped dependencies and annual tests exist, but exceptions are approved informally or availability trend is not reported.
questions.l5: Availability and continuity targets per service; critical dependencies mapped; plans tested at least annually with reports; exceptions approved and corrective actions tracked; availability trend reported monthly.
questions.remediation: Map every model provider, tool API and data store each orchestration service depends on, and set availability targets that account for the weakest dependency.
questions.text: Does the agent implement ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018 §8.6 by defining service continuity and availability targets for orchestration services, mapping critical dependencies (third parties and internal components), testing continuity/availability plans, managing exceptions, and producing evidence packs (targets, test reports, corrective actions, and trend metrics)?

questions.failureMode: The agent auto-closes incidents it cannot resolve, inflating its success rate while MTTR for real recoveries rises unmeasured.
questions.l1: No ITIL practice operationalization: no practice KPIs, runbooks, or continual improvement evidence
questions.l2: Incident handling follows habit; there is no practice owner and no KPIs.
questions.l3: Some ITIL-like processes exist, but KPIs, ownership, and evidence outputs are incomplete or inconsistent
questions.l4: Owned KPIs, runbooks and an improvement backlog exist, but evidence of sustained execution over several periods is missing.
questions.l5: Full ITIL practice operationalization with owned KPIs, runbooks, continual improvement, and audit-ready evidence demonstrating sustained execution
questions.remediation: Name a practice owner, publish MTTR, availability and drill-success KPIs for agent-run services, and review the improvement backlog monthly.
questions.text: Does the agent operationalize the ITIL v4 §5.2.7 practice expectations by defining practice ownership, KPIs (availability, incident MTTR, recovery drill success), runbooks/workflows, continual improvement backlog, and evidence outputs that demonstrate the practice is executed and improved over time for orchestration services?

questions.failureMode: The agent applies a superseded clause when routing a cross-border transaction and picks the laxer jurisdiction's rule because the mapping drifted.
questions.l1: No mapping governance: citations drift and controls are not traceably anchored
questions.l2: Control citations were copied into a spreadsheet once and never revisited.
questions.l3: Mapping exists but review/versioning is manual and can lag updates
questions.l4: The mapping is versioned and reviewed, but no automated check flags controls whose cited clause changed.
questions.l5: Strong mapping governance with versioning, periodic review, and checks that controls cite the Council-required anchors consistently
questions.remediation: Version the control-to-clause map, run a CI check that every control cites a mapped article, and log each periodic review.
questions.text: Does the program maintain a versioned control-to-clause mapping (DORA/ISO/ITIL/GDPR) with periodic review, so each question/control is anchored to the exact Council-required article/section and evidence expectations remain audit-defensible over time?

questions.failureMode: The agent depends on a model provider outside the third-party register, so a provider outage halts a critical function with no tested exit.
questions.l1: AI service providers not in the ICT third-party register and no Art. 30 clauses.
questions.l2: AI providers are used under click-through terms and are absent from the third-party register.
questions.l3: Providers registered and assessed; contracts lack some Art. 30 provisions, or no exit strategy for providers supporting critical or important functions.
questions.l4: Every provider is registered with an Art. 30 clause map, but exit strategies are documented and never tested.
questions.l5: Every AI service provider in the register with a risk assessment; contracts mapped clause by clause to Art. 30; exit strategies documented and tested for providers supporting critical or important functions.
questions.regulatoryRef: EU DORA Art. 28; EU DORA Art. 30
questions.remediation: Add each model and AI tool provider to the ICT third-party register, map their contracts to Art. 30, and test the exit to an alternative provider.
questions.text: Does the financial entity manage ICT third-party risk for AI service providers in the orchestration chain under EU DORA Art. 28, with contracts containing the key contractual provisions of Art. 30 and documented exit strategies?
